title: Ban invented spokespeople, experts and narrators from every page
hypothesis: If every named or implied person on a page is real and consenting, then legal risk and buyer distrust both go down because no claim can be traced to a fake identity.
does_not_apply_when: A page only uses editorial third-person voice with no named person

signal.check: A live or planned page names or implies a doctor, expert, founder, patient or narrator whose identity or consent is not on file.

risk.note: Removing a fake person may need a rewrite of the proof section, but skipping this carries real legal and trust risk.

prerequisites: A list of every named or implied person on the page
Consent on file for any real person quoted or shown
steps: List every named or implied person on the page: author, expert, doctor, narrator, reviewer.
Check each one is real, consenting, qualified where implied, and disclosed.
Rewrite any invented or unverifiable person as clear editorial third-person voice.
File written consent for any real person the page quotes or shows.
Re-run this check whenever a new draft adds a person.

test.method: Run the compliance checklist before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch and after every copy change that adds a person

title: Ban invented testimonials, reviews and comment sections
hypothesis: If every testimonial and review on a page is a real, unedited customer quote, then buyers trust the proof more and the brand avoids a platform or legal takedown.

signal.check: A page shows a testimonial, review, or comment with no matching real customer record, or a review copied from another site.

risk.note: Cutting a fake review may shrink the proof section; a real one should replace it, not leave a gap.

prerequisites: A review export with name, platform, date and consent status
steps: List every testimonial and review on the page with its source.
Confirm each one is a real customer, in their own words, with consent for name and photo use.
Remove any written persona, AI-generated quote, or review copied from a competitor.
Replace a removed fake review with a real one that answers the same objection.
Never write or edit a customer's words to fit a claim.

test.method: Run the compliance checklist before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Add a clear ad or sponsored disclosure label to every advertorial and quiz page
hypothesis: If every advertorial, presell and quiz page carries a clear ad label in the market's required form, then the brand avoids platform penalties and does not lose trust when a reader spots the ad.
does_not_apply_when: A storefront PDP or a direct product landing page with no editorial framing

signal.check: An advertorial, presell or quiz page has no visible ad label, or hides the brand behind a review-team or news-style name.

risk.note: Adding a label is a small, safe change; skipping it risks a platform takedown.

prerequisites: Current disclosure wording rules for the market checked
steps: Check the market's current disclosure wording rules for native advertising.
Add the label at the top of the page in the required form.
Make sure the brand or author is honestly named, never a fake review team or news masthead.
Repeat the disclosure near the bottom of long pages.
Re-check this on every new advertorial, presell or quiz page before launch.

test.method: Run the compliance checklist before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Audit every claim, number and endorsement against the brand's proof file before launch
hypothesis: If every number, endorsement and result claim on a page is checked against the brand's substantiated claims list before launch, then the brand ships fewer claims it cannot defend and avoids a platform or legal flag.

signal.check: A page draft contains a number, study, the word only, a guarantee, or a press mention with no matching record in the brand file.

risk.note: Cutting an unverified claim may weaken a headline; replace it with a claim the brand can prove.

prerequisites: Substantiated claims list from the brand record
Banned claims list for the category and market
steps: List every number, endorsement, study, the word only, a sold-out line, and every press mention on the page.
Match each one to a record in the brand's substantiated claims list.
Cut or rewrite any claim with no matching record.
Check health, safety, result and comparative claims against the category and market's rules.
Check every study cited traces to a real institution, population and result.
Log open items as needs-brand-data until they are resolved.

test.method: Run this audit before every launch and after every copy change that adds a number or claim.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Compute every saving, percentage and lift number in code, never from memory
hypothesis: If every saving, discount percentage and lift figure shown on a page is computed from the real price and order data, then the numbers stay accurate and match the cart every time.

signal.check: A page shows a saving, percentage, or lift number typed by hand instead of pulled from price or order data.

risk.note: A hand-typed number can drift from the real price after a price change; compute it live or at build time instead.

prerequisites: Price and bundle data available to the page or build script
steps: Find every saving, percentage, or lift number on the page.
Replace any hand-typed number with one computed from the real price, cost or order data.
Match the computed saving to what the cart actually charges.
Re-check after any price or bundle change.

test.method: Compare the shown saving to the cart total on a test order before launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch and after any price change

title: Use competitor and swipe pages for structure and mood only, never copy their content
hypothesis: If competitor pages and swipe files are used only for structure, section order and mood, then the brand gets a faster draft without copying text, claims, images, logos or products it does not own.

signal.check: A draft page's copy, claims, images or layout can be traced word for word or image for image to a competitor's live page.

risk.note: Skipping this risks a copyright or trademark problem, not a sales loss.

prerequisites: A folder of competitor pages and swipe files collected for reference
steps: Collect competitor and category pages for section order, pacing and mood only.
Never copy their exact text, claims, names, images, faces or products.
Write all copy from the brand's own facts and research.
Note the run date of any ad library reference to confirm the swipe is still live and typical.

test.method: Compare the final draft against the reference page for copied text or images before launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Only use before-and-after images that are real and allowed in the category
hypothesis: If every before-and-after image on a page is a real, unstaged result and the category allows the format, then the brand avoids a platform flag and does not mislead the buyer.
does_not_apply_when: A category where before-and-after images are restricted or banned by the market

signal.check: A page or planned page shows a before-and-after image with no real record behind it, or the category restricts the format.

risk.note: Health and beauty categories often regulate this format; check before shooting or publishing.

prerequisites: Category rules on before-and-after images checked for the market
steps: Check whether the category and market allow before-and-after images.
Confirm each before-and-after image is a real, unstaged customer result on file.
Cut any staged or generated before-and-after image.
Add the required disclaimer if the market requires one.

test.method: Run the compliance checklist before every launch of a page with this image type.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Rewrite copy that asserts a personal health, weight or financial state about the reader
hypothesis: If copy avoids asserting a reader's health, weight or financial state directly, then the page stays inside ad platform policy and does not feel invasive to the reader.

signal.check: Copy reads like you are overweight or your liver is clogged instead of naming the general problem.

risk.note: A softened line still needs to keep the same persuasive point; test the rewrite.

prerequisites: Current ad platform policy on personal attributes checked
steps: Search the draft for lines that assert a health, weight, or financial state about the reader.
Rewrite each one to name the problem or desire without asserting a personal state.
Check the rewrite against the ad platform's current personal attributes policy.
Keep the same persuasive point in a policy-safe form.

test.method: Run the compliance checklist before every launch of ad-facing copy.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Keep API keys and secrets out of page JavaScript
hypothesis: If every API key and secret a page uses lives on the backend and never in page JavaScript, then a leaked page cannot expose the brand's credentials.

signal.check: A page's source code, custom HTML block or theme file contains an API key, token or password in plain text.

risk.note: A leaked key can be used by someone else until it is rotated; treat any exposure as urgent.

prerequisites: A backend or server environment able to hold environment variables
steps: Check the page source for any API key, token or password.
Move any found secret to a backend environment variable.
Confirm the host's environment variables are set before the page goes live.
Re-check page source after every build or template change.

test.method: View page source and search for key-like strings before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Send high-intent, returning or visually simple product traffic straight to the PDP
hypothesis: If retargeting, branded search, cart abandoners and simple self-evident products go straight to the PDP, then conversion rate rises because these visitors want price and the buy box, not education.
does_not_apply_when: Cold, unaware traffic to a product that needs explaining

signal.check: Retargeting, branded search, or cart-abandoner traffic is routed through an advertorial or long landing page instead of the PDP, or a simple, visible-value product sends cold traffic anywhere but the PDP.

risk.note: Routing is a link change; revert if conversion falls.

prerequisites: Traffic mix by source and awareness stage per page
steps: List every traffic source and its awareness stage: retargeting, branded search, cart abandoners, repeat buyers.
Point each of these directly at the PDP.
For a visually simple, self-evident product, send cold traffic to the PDP too.
Track conversion rate and CPA on the direct-to-PDP path.

test.method: Compare purchase rate and CPA on direct-to-PDP traffic against any educating-page alternative on the same audience.
test.read_point: After a full weekly cycle of the routing

title: Put an educating page between the ad and the PDP for cold or skeptical traffic
hypothesis: If cold or unaware traffic to a product that needs explaining lands on an advertorial, presell, quiz or long landing page first, then conversion rises because the visitor understands the offer before reaching price.
does_not_apply_when: A simple, visible-value product on cold traffic, which should route to the PDP instead

signal.check: Cold Meta traffic on a product needing about 3 minutes of explanation, a new mechanism, or a crowded category is routed straight to the PDP with a low purchase rate.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source tests this route against direct-to-PDP on the same traffic

risk.note: Building an educating page costs time; test it against direct-to-PDP on the same audience before scaling it.

prerequisites: Cold-traffic PDP conversion rate and CPA to compare against
A research base or a winning ad angle
steps: Confirm the product needs real explanation: a new mechanism, a skeptical market, or a claim that needs unpacking.
Choose the page type: advertorial, presell, quiz, or long landing page.
Build the page from a research base or a proven ad angle, not a guess.
Split the route against direct-to-PDP on the same cold audience.
Judge the test on purchase rate and CPA, not click-through.

test.method: Split cold traffic between the educating page and the PDP.
test.read_point: After the traffic floor set for this page is reached

title: Build the advertorial only after a winning ad or a written research base exists
hypothesis: If an advertorial is built only after an ad has proven the angle at break-even or a full research base is written, then the page rests on evidence instead of a guess, and fewer pages get scrapped.
does_not_apply_when: A new brand with no ad history, where a declared research-stage page replaces the ad-proof gate

signal.check: A team is about to write a full advertorial with no ad results and no research documents on file.

risk.note: Delaying the advertorial build costs time, not money; skipping the gate risks wasted copywriting hours.

prerequisites: An ad that has run and converted at or near break-even, or a completed research base
steps: Check whether an ad has proven the angle at or near break-even, confirming avatar, desire, angle and mechanism.
If no ad has proven the angle, confirm a full research base exists before drafting.
If neither exists, mark the page as research-stage only and route budget to angle testing first.
Log the break-even ROAS and spend used to prove the angle.

test.method: Track advertorial win rate against whether it was built after ad proof or not.
test.read_point: After the first 5 advertorials tracked this way

title: Pick the advertorial format by the buyer's main obstacle, not by habit
hypothesis: If the advertorial format is picked to match the buyer's main obstacle, such as low trust, need for permission, too many options, or fit doubt, then the page speaks to the real blocker instead of a generic template.

signal.check: Research shows a specific buyer obstacle, such as distrust, overwhelm, or fit doubt, but the planned advertorial uses a generic story format that does not address it.

risk.note: Choosing the wrong format wastes a draft, not money.

prerequisites: Research naming the buyer's main obstacle
steps: Name the buyer's main obstacle from research: low trust, need for permission, too many options, or fit doubt.
Match it to a format: a story with early proof for low trust; a real expert for permission; a buyer's guide or comparison for overwhelm; a direct case-study frame for fit doubt.
For an improvement product, use a failed-solutions personal story; for an innovation, use a breaking-news or revelation frame.
Confirm the chosen frame can be held to the end.

test.method: Compare purchase rate across 2 formats for the same product and audience.
test.read_point: After each format reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Classify each page's traffic awareness stage before writing the top of the page
hypothesis: If the awareness stage of a page's traffic is named before writing, then the hero and pain placement match what the visitor already knows, and fewer visitors bounce confused or bored.

signal.check: A page brief has no stated awareness stage, or 2 pages fed by very different traffic use the same hero and pain placement.

risk.note: This is a planning step; it does not change a live page by itself.

prerequisites: Traffic mix by source per page
Customer survey or notes on prior category knowledge, where available
steps: Read the traffic source for the page: Meta cold, Meta retargeting, Google search, SEO, or email.
Classify the awareness stage: unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, or most-aware.
For a new category, read the market stage from search trend history: clueless, curious, or saturated.
Record the stage and its source in the page brief before writing the hero.
Re-classify if the feeding ad or channel changes.

test.method: Compare conversion rate on pages where the stage was named against pages where it was guessed.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Use a quiz funnel when product choice or belief needs a few real answers first
hypothesis: If cold traffic in a real problem-solution category gets a quiz that personalises the path and collects first-party research, then conversion and research quality both improve because the recommendation is real and the team reads the answers.
does_not_apply_when: Gifting, fashion or jewellery, where no source shows a quiz working
A single-product brand with no real recommendation to make

signal.check: The brand has a product range or plan where the right pick genuinely depends on the buyer's answers, and the team is willing to export and read quiz answers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client went from 2.3% to over 3%, not isolated from other changes

risk.note: A quiz with no real branching just adds friction; test quiz-path conversion against direct-to-PDP.

prerequisites: A product range or plan where answers change the recommendation
Team commitment to export and read quiz answers
steps: Confirm the category is problem-solution and a real recommendation exists.
Confirm the team will export and read the answers regularly.
Build the quiz spec from the research base.
Test quiz-path purchase rate and RPV against direct-to-PDP on the same traffic.

test.method: Split traffic between the quiz path and direct-to-PDP.
test.read_point: After the quiz reaches about 100 submissions

title: Use a sales page, order page and post-purchase offers for outcome-led, high-AOV consumables
hypothesis: If a consumable or course-style product with a natural next problem gets a full sales page, a low-friction order page and a post-purchase offer, then AOV and contribution per buyer both rise because the funnel sells more than one item per visit.
does_not_apply_when: One-off durable goods with no natural next problem

signal.check: The product is a consumable, supplement or course with a real next problem, but the funnel today stops at a single-item PDP with native checkout.

risk.note: Leaving native checkout can lose accelerated wallets and speed; weigh that trade-off before building a custom order page.

prerequisites: COGS per SKU and contribution per buyer from finance
Platform support for a custom order page and post-purchase offers, verified in the UI
steps: Map the current flow and drop-off per step before any redesign.
Write the sales page with a scored headline, real urgency, real scarcity, a real guarantee, a named mechanism, and objection-matched testimonials.
Build the order page with obvious card fields, quantity breaks, and 1 or 2 order bumps priced by real contribution.
Add a post-purchase offer at peak emotion, priced by contribution per buyer, routed to a down-sell on no.
Split test the order page first, then the post-purchase offer and price.

test.method: Compare AOV and contribution per buyer before and after the funnel change.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Build a fast, low-persuasion reorder path for repeat and loyalty customers
hypothesis: If a returning, logged-in or matched customer skips the hero persuasion and sees their past order with a 1-click reorder, then repeat purchase rate rises because the path is shorter and does not resell what they already believe.
does_not_apply_when: A store with no login, loyalty cookie or email match to identify a returning customer

signal.check: Repeat and loyalty customers land on the same persuasion-heavy page as cold traffic, with no shortcut to reorder.

risk.note: Verify against the brand's own repeat-purchase data before building; no library source backs this.

prerequisites: A way to match a returning customer: login, email match, or loyalty cookie
steps: Identify a returning, logged-in customer or one matched by email or loyalty cookie.
Cut hero persuasion and proof sections for this path.
Surface their past order and its quantity.
Offer 1-click reorder or resubscribe.
Shorten the remaining path to checkout.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase rate and time-to-reorder before and after the shortcut path.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Mirror the ad's exact promise in the page's hero headline
hypothesis: If the hero headline repeats the ad's exact promise, persona and offer, then conversion rises because the visitor does not lose the benefit that earned the click.

signal.check: The page's hero headline is a generic brand line while the feeding ad made a specific, different promise.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the most agreed rule in the folder but no isolated number is given

risk.note: A headline swap is fast to test and revert.

prerequisites: The live ad's exact promise, persona and offer, pasted into the brief
steps: Open the live ad and read its exact promise, persona and offer.
Write the hero headline to repeat that promise, not a generic brand line.
Check the headline against the ad side by side before launch.
Re-check whenever the ad's creative changes.

test.method: Compare bounce rate and conversion rate before and after the headline match.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Continue the ad's story in the page's opening; never start a new one
hypothesis: If the page's first screen closes the loop the ad opened, in the same voice, then conversion rises because the visitor feels the page is the next part of the same story, not a new pitch.

signal.check: The ad breaks a pattern, opens a loop, or teases a mechanism, but the page's opening restarts with unrelated copy.

risk.note: Rewriting the opening paragraph is low cost to test.

prerequisites: The ad's exact hook, loop and tone written down
steps: Read the ad's 4 jobs: pattern break, open loop, audience qualifier, mechanism tease.
Write the page's first screen to close that same loop in the same voice.
Check that the page does not introduce a new angle or tone.
Test a strong page behind the wrong ad against the same page behind the right ad, if traffic allows.

test.method: Read the ad and page opening side by side before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch and after any ad change

title: Keep one persona consistent from ad to page to PDP
hypothesis: If the same age, gender, problem and problem length carry through the ad, the headline, the story and the PDP copy, then conversion rises because the mirror never breaks.
does_not_apply_when: A catalogue store serving many segments on the same generic page

signal.check: The ad targets 1 clear persona but the page copy widens to everyone, or the PDP describes a different buyer.

risk.note: A copy edit; low cost.

prerequisites: The ad's persona: age band, gender if relevant, problem, and problem length
steps: Write down the ad's persona: age band, gender if relevant, problem, and problem length.
Check the headline, story and PDP copy all speak to that same persona.
Cut any line that widens the copy to everyone.
Use 1 archetype per advertorial rather than several.

test.method: Read the full funnel for persona drift before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Match page length and selling load to how much the feeding ad already sold
hypothesis: If a click-only ad gets a long lead with the product revealed later, and a long ad or VSL gets a short page with the product up front, then conversion rises because the page picks up the selling load where the ad left off.

signal.check: A clickbait image ad with no body copy sends traffic to a page that shows the product in the first lines, or a long-copy ad sends traffic to a page with a long lead before the product.

risk.note: Hedged by its own source as not always true; test before committing budget.

prerequisites: The feeding ad's format and copy length rated
steps: Rate the feeding ad: click-only image, long-copy native ad, or a video or VSL.
For a click-only ad, write a longer lead with the product revealed later in the page.
For a long-copy ad or VSL, put the product in the first lines of the page.
Decide the reveal point from this rating and record it in the draft plan.
Treat the first-proof-block position as a test variable once format and headline are set.

test.method: Split test 2 lead lengths on the same ad and audience where traffic allows.
test.read_point: After the page reaches its traffic floor

title: Build a separate page per keyword or ad angle, not 1 catch-all page
hypothesis: If each search keyword or paid social angle gets its own URL, then message match holds for every visitor and conversion rate rises because no single page tries to serve 2 different promises.
does_not_apply_when: Publishing thousands of near-identical pages in a short window, which risks a search policy problem

signal.check: Several distinct keywords or ad angles all send traffic to the same 1 landing page.

risk.note: Too many near-duplicate pages published at once can trigger a search policy problem; check current rules first.

prerequisites: Current search engine policy on scaled or programmatic pages checked
steps: List every distinct keyword or ad angle sending traffic to the store.
Build a separate URL for each one, refined to that angle's promise.
Check current search policy before publishing many pages at once.
Route each ad or keyword to its matching page.

test.method: Compare conversion rate per angle before and after splitting into separate pages.
test.read_point: After a full test cycle per page

title: Match the ad's CTA label to where it sends traffic
hypothesis: If an ad to an advertorial uses Learn More and an ad to a quiz uses Take the Quiz, then click-through quality rises because the visitor knows what happens next before they click.

signal.check: An ad sends traffic to a presell or quiz page but uses a Shop Now or Buy Now button.

risk.note: This is an ad setting change; hand it to the ad deployment owner.

prerequisites: Agreement on which page each ad sends to
steps: Check where each ad currently sends traffic: PDP, advertorial, or quiz.
Set the CTA label to Learn More for an advertorial or presell.
Set the CTA label to Take the Quiz for a quiz.
Hand the CTA label change to the ad account owner.

test.method: Compare click-through quality and post-click conversion before and after the CTA label change.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Keep price, discount, guarantee and shipping identical from ad to page to cart to checkout
hypothesis: If the price, saving, guarantee and shipping terms match on every step from the ad to the final checkout, then conversion rises because the visitor never meets a broken promise.

signal.check: The ad states one discount or guarantee and the page, cart, or checkout states a different one.

risk.note: A copy fix; low cost to correct once found.

prerequisites: The live ad, page, cart and checkout screens open side by side
steps: List the price, discount, guarantee and shipping terms shown in the ad.
Compare them against the page, cart and checkout.
Fix the weaker or mismatched step so every step agrees.
Re-check on every price, offer or policy change.

test.method: Walk the full funnel from ad to checkout before every launch and after any offer change.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Re-run the message-match check whenever ad creative changes
hypothesis: If the message-match check re-runs every time the feeding ad's creative changes, then the page never drifts out of sync with a new ad promise or persona.

signal.check: An ad's headline, image, or offer has changed since the page's last message-match check.

risk.note: A recurring check; no downside.

prerequisites: A log of the current live ad creative per page
steps: Note the date of the page's last message-match check.
Watch for ad creative changes on every page that feeds traffic to it.
Re-run the message-match checklist whenever the ad's promise, persona, or offer changes.
Fix the page's hero if it no longer matches.

test.method: Schedule a message-match re-check on every ad creative refresh.
test.read_point: Within the first week after an ad creative change

title: Build the hero in a fixed 6-part order: proof, headline, subhead, CTA, FUD, image, second proof
hypothesis: If the first screen carries proof, benefit headline, subheadline, CTA, FUD reducers, a promise image, and a second proof line in that order, then conversion rises because the fold covers every trust and clarity check at once.
does_not_apply_when: A storefront PDP, which uses the PDP first-screen spec instead

signal.check: The hero is missing 1 or more of proof, headline, subhead, CTA, FUD, or image, or they appear in a different order.

risk.note: A hero rebuild ships as a test variant, not a blind swap.

prerequisites: A completed pre-build page brief
steps: List the 6 hero parts: proof 1, benefit headline, subheadline, CTA, FUD reducers, promise image, proof 2.
Draft each part from the page brief.
Arrange them in the fixed order.
Check the mobile fold shows all 6 parts, or as many as fit, before the first scroll.
Ship the new hero as a test variant against the current live hero.

test.method: A/B test the new hero against the current one.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Write the headline as the outcome this SKU delivers, never the category or an invented number
hypothesis: If the headline states what this exact SKU delivers for the buyer, backed only by numbers the brand's own record supports, then conversion rises because the visitor sees what is in it for them instead of a category label.

signal.check: The headline states the product category, the brand name, or a number the brand record cannot back.

risk.note: A copy edit.

prerequisites: Substantiated outcome and time claims from the brand record
steps: Write down the 1 outcome this SKU delivers, not the category it sits in.
Check every number in the draft against the brand's substantiated claims list.
Cut any invented number, even one used in a source example.
Run the 5-second test: does a new reader say what it is, what they gain, and why this brand.

test.method: Show the headline to someone new for 5 seconds and ask what the page sells.
test.read_point: Before shipping and again after launch

title: Pick a tested headline formula, then score it against the outcome rule
hypothesis: If the headline follows a proven formula, such as end result plus time plus emotional payoff, then it is more likely to pass the outcome and specificity checks than a headline written from scratch.

signal.check: The headline was written without testing it against any of the known formulas.

risk.note: Formula choice is free to test in copy.

prerequisites: Awareness stage of the traffic named
steps: Draft 5 to 10 headlines using different formulas: end result plus time plus payoff; 3 beats of outcome, credibility, fear removal; who, what, what's in it for me; a so-that chain; a contrarian claim for a curious market.
Mark which formula mirrors the ad promise and the awareness stage.
Score each on the 7-trait scale.
Keep the top scoring 1 or 2 for further testing.

test.method: Score each headline draft and A/B test the top 2.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Write the subheadline to explain how, never to repeat the headline
hypothesis: If the subheadline names the mechanism, proprietary method, or USP behind the headline's promise, then the hero earns more trust in the same space because it adds new information instead of repeating the headline.

signal.check: The subheadline restates the headline in different words instead of explaining how the outcome happens.

risk.note: A copy edit.

steps: Read the headline and subheadline together.
Rewrite the subheadline to name the mechanism, method, or USP, or run pain then solution.
Add an effort or risk clause if it fits the brand voice.
Confirm it does not repeat the headline's words or claim.

test.method: Read headline and subheadline together and check for repetition before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Keep hero body copy to 2 or 3 sentences or 3 to 4 bullets
hypothesis: If the hero body copy is cut to 2 to 3 sentences or 3 to 4 bullets, then more visitors read it because a cold visitor scans only a small share of the page.

signal.check: The hero body runs longer than 3 to 4 lines or bullets before the CTA.

risk.note: A copy trim.

steps: Read the current hero body copy.
Cut it to 2 to 3 sentences or 3 to 4 bullets.
Quantify only numbers the brand record backs.
Check the trimmed copy still states the core benefit.

test.method: Compare scroll depth and conversion before and after the trim.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Show 2 verifiable proof forms above the fold; hand-pick reviews when the count is thin
hypothesis: If the hero shows 2 relevant, verifiable proof forms, and a brand with about 30 reviews or fewer hand-picks 2 to 4 relevant ones instead of headlining the count, then trust rises without exposing a thin number.

signal.check: The hero has 1 or 0 proof forms, or a thin review count is headlined instead of hand-picked reviews.

risk.note: A layout and copy change.

prerequisites: Review export with count and rating
Press quotes with permission, where available
steps: Pick 2 proof forms: rating and count, customer count, a quantified result, a press quote, or real client logos.
Check the review count; below about 30, hand-pick 2 to 4 objection-matched reviews instead of headlining the count.
Use a 4.7 to 4.9 rating as it is rather than rounding up.
Confirm each proof form links to something verifiable, not a bare claim.

test.method: A/B test hero proof forms and review-count display.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Build 1 obvious, benefit-labeled CTA that passes the blur test
hypothesis: If the hero has 1 CTA labeled as an outcome or task, and it still stands out when the page is blurred, then click-through to the next step rises because there is no doubt what to do next.
does_not_apply_when: A page with 2 genuinely separate intents, such as a demo and a trial on a B2B page

signal.check: The blur test fails: no single element stands out, or the CTA reads Submit, Contact Us, or Shop Now with no benefit.

risk.note: A styling and copy change.

steps: Blur the page and check that the CTA is the one thing that stands out.
Label the CTA as an outcome or task, such as Get thicker hair now, not Submit or Shop Now alone.
On a PDP, use the task label the platform expects, such as Add to cart, with benefit copy near it.
Cut any second CTA that competes rather than supports; keep a real secondary intent visually subordinate.

test.method: Run the blur test on every new hero before launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Place real FUD reducers next to or under every CTA and add-to-cart button
hypothesis: If real, policy-backed reassurance lines, such as guarantee, return window, and shipping time, sit right under every CTA, then conversion rises because hesitation is answered at the moment of decision.

signal.check: A CTA or add-to-cart button has no reassurance line under it, or the line stated does not match the brand's real policy.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client reported 40 to 60 percent and another 30 percent, each on 1 client with no sample size

risk.note: Wording must match the real policy exactly; a mismatch is a compliance risk.

prerequisites: Real guarantee, return window, warranty, and shipping terms from the brand record
steps: Pull the real guarantee, return window, warranty, shipping cost and delivery time from the brand record.
Write each as a short reducer line: money-back guarantee, free returns, ships in 24 hours, secure checkout.
Place them directly under or beside every CTA and add-to-cart button.
Check each line matches the policy page word for word.

test.method: A/B test adding or repositioning FUD reducers under the CTA.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Fit the fixed PDP first-screen elements on the brand's main mobile device
hypothesis: If the first mobile screen of a PDP shows thumbnails, rating and count, title, price with any saving, the variant selector, add to cart, and FUD reducers, then more visitors reach add to cart because everything needed to buy fits before the first scroll.

signal.check: Add to cart, the rating, or the price sits below the first mobile screen, or dots replace visible thumbnails.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 store saw only about 36 percent scroll reach add to cart before the fix

risk.note: Keep the previous template version to revert if add-to-cart rate falls.

prerequisites: Scroll map and click share for the PDP
Bundle maths from the offer domain, if tiers are shown
steps: Replace pagination dots with visible thumbnails.
Move rating and review count near the title, linked to the on-page reviews.
Put title, price, any saving, the selector and add to cart above the first-screen line on the main device.
Shorten the description above the button and cut empty space.
Add FUD reducers directly under add to cart.
Check the scroll map after launch to confirm most visitors reach add to cart.

test.method: Read the scroll map before and after the rebuild.
test.read_point: After 2 to 4 weeks of traffic on the new template

title: Use a hero image or video that shows the promise, never a decoration
hypothesis: If the hero image or video shows a transformation, the product in use, or a proof collage instead of a mood shot, then conversion rises because a visitor who only looks at the image still understands what is sold.

signal.check: The hero image is a venue shot, generic stock photo, or a packshot with no context, and covering the copy leaves the visitor unsure what is sold.

risk.note: An image swap is easy to test and revert.

prerequisites: Real product photos or a real transformation image on file
steps: Hide the copy and look only at the current hero image; ask what is sold.
Choose an image type: a transformation, a happy user in the outcome state, the product in use, or a verified proof collage.
Use the real product photo wherever the product appears; never a generated or stock face as a real customer.
Test the new image against the current one where traffic allows.

test.method: A/B test the hero image against the current one.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Set a clear visual hierarchy: biggest headline, lighter body, accent-colour CTA
hypothesis: If the headline is clearly the largest and boldest element, the body is lighter and smaller, and the CTA sits in a distinct accent colour, then the visitor's eye lands on the right thing first, especially on mobile.

signal.check: The headline is close to body text size, everything is bold or all caps, or a logo or announcement bar buries the button on mobile.

risk.note: A styling change.

steps: Check the headline is at least 3 to 4 times the body text size, or clearly the largest element.
Give the body text a lighter weight and a second colour.
Put the CTA in 1 distinct accent colour used nowhere else.
Cut all-caps and bold from everywhere except the 1 or 2 elements meant to stand out.
Check the mobile fold for a headline, body, proof, and CTA that all fit without an oversized logo or bar.

test.method: Blur the page and check the hierarchy still reads correctly.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Cut empty white space between the fold and the first proof block
hypothesis: If spacing is tightened until headline, body, proof and CTA all fit within the average mobile fold, then fewer visitors leave before seeing any proof.

signal.check: A scroll map shows an empty gap right after the fold, or a steep drop in reach right after the average fold line.

risk.note: A spacing fix.

prerequisites: A scroll map for the page's main device
steps: Read the scroll map's average fold line.
Check that proof 2 sits above or right at that line.
Cut spacing between the headline, body, and proof until they fit the first screen without overwhelm.
Re-check the scroll map after the change.

test.method: Compare the scroll map before and after tightening spacing.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 weeks of traffic

title: Use a familiar page layout instead of a creative one when clarity is at stake
hypothesis: If the page follows a familiar conversion layout instead of a creative one, then fewer visitors are confused by 2 headlines, oversized proof, or a headline with no CTA nearby.
does_not_apply_when: A creative layout that has already been tested against a familiar control and won

signal.check: The page has 2 competing headlines, proof that dwarfs the headline, body copy far from the headline it supports, or a hero with no visible CTA.

risk.note: A layout fix, reversible.

steps: Compare the page against the standard 6-part hero pattern.
Flag any of the warning signs: 2 headlines, oversized proof, distant body copy, or a CTA-less hero.
Rebuild the layout to the familiar pattern.
If a creative layout is kept, test it against a familiar control.

test.method: A/B test the familiar layout against the creative one.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Use a form-above-the-fold hero only for high-intent search or branded traffic
hypothesis: If a form-above-the-fold hero is used only for Google search or branded traffic, and cold Meta traffic gets an education-first hero instead, then conversion rises because an early ask is never made before trust is earned.
does_not_apply_when: Cold paid social traffic, where asking before educating is premature

signal.check: Cold Meta traffic lands on a hero with an immediate form or buy ask and no context.

risk.note: A hero-variant routing decision by traffic source.

prerequisites: Traffic source known per page
steps: Check the traffic source feeding the page.
For Google search or branded traffic, use a hero with 1 benefit headline, 3 to 4 bullets, and 1 large CTA with a risk reducer.
For cold Meta traffic, use the education-first hero instead.
On a store, the equivalent for high-intent traffic is a direct buy-box PDP.

test.method: Compare conversion rate by traffic source and hero variant.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches its traffic floor

title: Add a subscribe-and-save selector to the PDP first screen for consumable SKUs
hypothesis: If a consumable or replenishable SKU shows a subscribe-and-save option next to add to cart with the saving stated in money, then subscription share rises because the choice is visible at the moment of decision.
does_not_apply_when: A one-off or non-replenishable SKU

signal.check: A consumable SKU has no subscribe-and-save option visible on the PDP first screen.

risk.note: Verify against brand data before use; no library source backs this.

prerequisites: Subscription pricing and saving maths from the offer domain
steps: Confirm the SKU is consumable or replenishable.
Add a subscribe-and-save selector next to the add-to-cart control.
Show the subscription saving in money, to the same standard as the bundle savings rule.
Test the selector's placement and default state.

test.method: Compare subscription share before and after adding the selector.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Show a delivery ETA or pincode serviceability check near the buy box
hypothesis: If a delivery ETA or a pincode serviceability check sits near the buy box in a market where delivery time or reach varies by area, then conversion rises because the buyer knows before checkout whether the product will arrive and when.
does_not_apply_when: A market with uniform, fast delivery everywhere

signal.check: The PDP gives no delivery time or area check, and support tickets show buyers asking about delivery before or after ordering.

risk.note: Verify against brand data before use; no library source backs this.

prerequisites: Delivery time and serviceable area data by pincode or region
steps: Confirm delivery time or reach varies by area for this store.
Add a delivery ETA or pincode check near the buy box, placed with the other FUD reducers.
Pull delivery time and serviceability from live logistics data, not a guess.
Test its effect on add to cart and drop-off at checkout.

test.method: Compare add to cart and checkout drop-off before and after adding the check.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Show the local payment methods the market actually uses beside the FUD reducers
hypothesis: If the PDP and checkout entry point show the payment methods the local market actually trusts, such as COD, UPI, EMI, or buy-now-pay-later, instead of a generic card-logo strip, then checkout conversion rises because the buyer sees their preferred way to pay.
does_not_apply_when: A market where card and wallet payments already dominate and a generic strip is accurate

signal.check: The PDP shows only a generic card-logo strip while the market's real payment mix leans on COD, UPI, EMI or similar.

risk.note: The returns and shipping card is a separate item; payment-method trust itself is unverified beyond this gap being named.

prerequisites: The market's real payment method mix
steps: Find the payment methods the local market actually uses most.
Replace or add to the generic card-logo strip with those methods.
Place the payment trust signals beside the other FUD reducers.
Test the change on checkout conversion.

test.method: Compare checkout conversion before and after showing local payment methods.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Place every PDP control right next to the element it changes
hypothesis: If a colour swatch, size selector, or other control sits right next to the image or element it changes, then fewer visitors scroll back and forth confused, and add-to-cart rate rises.

signal.check: Session recordings show visitors scrolling up and down between a control and the element it affects.

risk.note: A layout fix.

prerequisites: Session recordings for the PDP
steps: Watch session recordings for scroll-up-and-down loops around a control.
Move the control, such as a colour swatch, next to the image or price it changes.
Re-check recordings after the fix to confirm the loop stops.

test.method: Compare recordings for the scroll-loop pattern before and after moving the control.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 weeks of traffic

title: Order a cold landing page: hero, pain, proof, value props, comparison, guarantee, FAQ, closer
hypothesis: If a cold-traffic landing page follows hero, pain section, proof block, several value prop sections, comparison, how-it-works, guarantee, more proof, FAQ, and a closer, with a CTA in every critical section, then conversion rises because the visitor is walked through education before being asked to buy.
does_not_apply_when: Warm or solution-aware traffic, which uses the shorter solution-aware order instead

signal.check: A cold-traffic page has 1 or 2 sections, skips pain and proof, or asks for the sale before any value prop.

risk.note: Ships as a new page or a tested variant; keep the old page live to revert.

prerequisites: A completed pre-build page brief
A research base for the pain section
steps: Confirm the traffic is cold and problem-aware.
Order the page: hero, pain section, a proof block, 3 to 4 value prop sections minimum (more for complex offers), a second proof block, a comparison block, how it works in 3 or 4 steps.
After that: a guarantee block if a guarantee exists, another proof block, an FAQ from real objections, and a closer.
Add a CTA to every critical section.
Write down the order and the awareness reason in the brief.

test.method: A/B test the new section order against the current page.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Shorten a solution-aware landing page: proof up top, pain small, buy action near the hero
hypothesis: If a page fed by search, branded, or retargeting traffic moves proof right under the hero, shrinks the pain section, and puts the buy or lead action near the top, then conversion rises because a warm visitor does not need to be re-educated.
does_not_apply_when: Cold, unaware traffic, which needs the full pain-and-education order instead

signal.check: A page fed by search or retargeting traffic uses the same long, education-heavy order as a cold landing page.

risk.note: A section-order rebuild ships as a test variant.

prerequisites: Traffic source confirmed as solution-aware or warmer
steps: Confirm the traffic is search, branded, or retargeting.
Move proof right under the hero.
Shrink the pain section and move it below the proof.
Let value props follow, with the buy or lead action available near the hero.

test.method: A/B test the shortened order against the long cold-traffic order on warm traffic.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Build a dedicated ecommerce campaign page order for a single product on paid traffic
hypothesis: If a dedicated single-product campaign page puts the selector and add-to-cart with FUD reducers near the top, then image-led value props, comparison, a routine block, reviews and FAQ, then conversion and RPV both rise because the buy action is never buried under long-form copy.
does_not_apply_when: A general storefront PDP template, which uses the PDP-specific order instead

signal.check: A dedicated campaign page for 1 product buries the selector and add-to-cart below several sections of copy.

risk.note: No source shows a fully tested store order for this page type; treat it as a starting hypothesis.

prerequisites: Bundle maths and price data from the offer domain
steps: Open with hero: product, benefit headline, proof, price and offer.
Place the selector and add to cart with FUD reducers near the top.
Add image-led value props with proof scattered between them.
Add a comparison against real alternatives, a 3 or 4 step routine block, a review grid, and an FAQ.
Close with a second buy block.
Make add to cart open a cart drawer, not a page reload.

test.method: A/B test the campaign page order against the current one.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Order the PDP body below the first screen: modules, objection reviews, specs, FAQ
hypothesis: If the PDP body below the first screen runs benefit modules with real imagery, objection-matched reviews near the buy box, a full open review section on mobile, FUD reducers at drop-off points, and specs kept scannable, then more visitors who scroll past the first screen still convert.

signal.check: The PDP body is a wall of dense text, reviews are buried or hidden in an accordion, or specs are missing.

risk.note: Keep the previous template version to revert.

prerequisites: PDP first-screen spec already in place
steps: Convert dense text blocks into icon-and-image benefit modules.
Place objection-matched reviews near the buy box and open a full review section on mobile.
Add FUD reducers between sections at steep drop-off points.
Keep size, care, ingredients and specs available in a scannable form.
Build the FAQ from support tickets and reviews for this SKU.
Keep store navigation reachable.

test.method: Compare scroll-through and conversion before and after the body rebuild.
test.read_point: After 2 to 4 weeks of traffic

title: Fix homepage and collection pages to raise View Product Rate without hurting add to cart
hypothesis: If the homepage headline states the shopper benefit, navigation shows visual categories ordered by click share, and the collection page consolidates products above the fold with honest badges, then View Product Rate rises without a fall in add-to-cart or purchase rate.
does_not_apply_when: A single hero-SKU brand with almost no browse traffic

signal.check: The homepage headline is a slogan, the nav buries the shop menu, or the collection page pushes products below several rows of banners.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client each reported plus 15 percent and plus 72 percent, no sample size

risk.note: Menu and template versions are kept; revert on a fall in add to cart or purchase over a full cycle.

prerequisites: GA4 path exploration and landing page report
Area map data for the homepage and collection
steps: Measure View Product Rate, add-to-cart rate, and purchase rate, computed in code.
Rewrite the homepage headline as the shopper benefit and match the lead image to it.
Cut the nav to 7 items or fewer: remove near-zero-click items, remove Home, move About, Contact, Blog and FAQ to a sub-menu or footer.
Add product images or story-style icons to the nav or a category row near the top, ordered by click share.
On the collection page, consolidate above-the-fold content, use 1 or 2 filter layers, and show honest Best Seller badges.
Test quick add on the collection where reverse-path data shows many add-to-carts after collection to PDP.
Re-check path loops, such as home to collection to home, after launch.

test.method: Compare View Product Rate, add-to-cart, and purchase rate before and after the fixes.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Open cold-traffic pages on the exact shopping friction this SKU solves, not a generic pain dump
hypothesis: If the page opens on the exact friction this SKU removes, in a format that fits the offer, such as a before-and-after, a sales-letter PAS, or a short PAS, then the visitor recognises their own problem and reads on instead of bouncing.
does_not_apply_when: High-intent visitors, where the pain section is shortened or skipped

signal.check: The page's opening pain section is generic, invents harm, makes a medical claim, or lists pain with no agitation and no solution.

risk.note: Agitation must stay honest and fit the brand voice; a curiosity-and-proof lead can be tested against a pain lead in crowded categories.

prerequisites: Research naming the SKU's specific friction point
Brand voice rules and limits on agitation
steps: Name the exact friction this SKU removes: a stain, a leak, a return trip, a specific daily annoyance.
Pick the format: a graphical before-and-after for visual transformations, a sales-letter PAS for complex offers, or a short PAS for simple offers.
Write problem, honest agitation, then the solution as the clear way out.
Check the agitation invents no harm and makes no medical claim.
Test a curiosity-and-proof lead against the pain lead in a crowded category.

test.method: A/B test 2 opener formats on the same traffic.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Write each value prop section as a benefit heading with the feature as support
hypothesis: If each value prop section drills the feature down to the day-to-day benefit with a so-what or so-that chain, then a visitor who reads only the headings is still sold, because the copy leads with what the buyer gets.

signal.check: A value prop section leads with a feature or spec name instead of the benefit it produces.

risk.note: A copy rewrite.

steps: List every value prop section and its current heading.
Drill each feature with so what or so that until a day-to-day benefit appears.
Rewrite the heading as that benefit, with the feature as supporting text.
Add 1 clear image per section that matches the benefit.

test.method: Read only the headings top to bottom and check they sell on their own.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Show how the product works in 3 or 4 steps that end at the outcome
hypothesis: If a how-it-works block breaks the product's use into 3 or 4 steps ending in the outcome, then a skeptical visitor pictures the routine and the outcome together, which lowers hesitation.
does_not_apply_when: A product with no process or routine to show

signal.check: The page has no how-it-works block, or the block stops at the last action instead of the outcome.

risk.note: A copy and layout addition.

steps: Break the product's use into 3 or 4 steps.
Make the last step the end benefit, not the last action.
Add a short image or icon per step.
Adapt the framing to how the product fits the customer's existing routine.

test.method: A/B test adding or reworking the how-it-works block.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Build an honest comparison block against the 2 or 3 real alternatives shoppers actually weigh
hypothesis: If the comparison block names the real SKUs or brands a shopper is price-checking, with an accurate checks-and-crosses table, then hesitant comparison shoppers convert instead of leaving to check elsewhere.
does_not_apply_when: A category with no real close alternative shoppers weigh

signal.check: Shoppers frequently compare this SKU to 2 or 3 specific alternatives, but the page has no comparison block or an inaccurate one.

risk.note: Every comparison must be accurate and honest about where a rival may fit better; check comparative advertising rules for the market.

prerequisites: Research on which 2 or 3 alternatives shoppers actually compare
Current comparative advertising rules for the market
steps: Identify the 2 or 3 SKUs or brands shoppers actually compare in the same search or listing.
Build a checks-and-crosses table with a line of text per cell for complex offers.
Check every claim in the table is accurate.
Admit where a rival may suit a different buyer better.
Check current comparative advertising rules for the market before publishing.

test.method: A/B test adding the comparison block.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: End long pages with a mini-hero closer, not a Contact Us line
hypothesis: If the page ends with a mini hero that recaps the outcome, gives 1 reason to act today, restates proof and FUD, and repeats the CTA, then visitors who scrolled the whole page get one more clear chance to buy.
does_not_apply_when: A short PDP with a sticky buy module, which may not need a separate closer

signal.check: The page ends with Contact Us, Want to know more, or no CTA at all.

risk.note: A copy addition at the end of the page.

steps: Write a closer with a benefit headline that recaps the dream outcome.
Add 1 final reason to act today.
Restate 3 value props or 3 to 5 bullets, 2 proof forms, and the FUD reducers.
For a store, end with the product selector and add to cart again.

test.method: A/B test adding or rewriting the closer section.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Build the PDP FAQ from that SKU's own tickets, negative reviews and searches
hypothesis: If the PDP FAQ is built from that specific SKU's support tickets, negative reviews and on-site search, not a site-wide FAQ, then it answers the real objections stopping a purchase instead of acting as filler.

signal.check: The PDP FAQ is the same generic block used site-wide, or its questions do not trace to a real ticket, review, or search query for this SKU.

risk.note: A content build from existing data; low cost.

prerequisites: Support tickets, negative reviews, and on-site search queries for this SKU
steps: Pull support tickets, negative reviews, and on-site search queries for this SKU.
Ask sales or support whether anything was ambiguous for this product.
Write FAQ questions that trace to a real ticket, call note, or review.
Place a matching testimonial or copy line earlier on the page so the objection never has to reach the FAQ.
Keep this FAQ separate from the site-wide FAQ.

test.method: Compare ticket volume for this SKU before and after the FAQ rebuild.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Turn on-site search into a conversion lever, not just a box
hypothesis: If on-site search handles synonyms and typos, ranks results by margin and stock, and logs every unmatched query, then more search users find the right product and the store learns what shoppers are asking for.
does_not_apply_when: A single-SKU store with no meaningful on-site search volume

signal.check: On-site search returns no or poor results for common misspellings or synonyms, or unmatched queries are never reviewed.

risk.note: The feature itself has no library source; verify against the store's own search log.

prerequisites: Search log with query volume and result counts
steps: Pull the on-site search log and find the most common zero-result or poor-result queries.
Add synonyms and typo tolerance for the top queries.
Merchandise results by margin and stock where ties exist.
Feed unmatched queries into the objection-mining process.

test.method: Track zero-result search rate and search-to-purchase rate before and after the fixes.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Add a frequently-bought-together module for a real, commonly co-purchased companion item
hypothesis: If a PDP shows a frequently-bought-together module for a genuinely common companion item, then AOV rises because the suggestion matches what buyers already do, not an unrelated add-on.
does_not_apply_when: A SKU with no real, commonly co-purchased companion item

signal.check: Order data shows a SKU is commonly bought with a specific companion item, but the PDP has no module suggesting it.

risk.note: The module itself has no library source; base the companion choice on real co-purchase data.

prerequisites: Order data showing real co-purchase patterns
steps: Pull order data to find SKUs genuinely and commonly bought together.
Add a frequently-bought-together module on the PDP, separate from the cart-drawer cross-sell.
Never suggest an unrelated add-on.
Track AOV and units per order before and after.

test.method: Compare AOV on PDPs with and without the module.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Add a dedicated size or fit guide module for any SKU with a sizing decision
hypothesis: If apparel, footwear, or any SKU with a sizing decision gets a dedicated size or fit guide module on the PDP, then fewer buyers guess wrong, which should lower returns from wrong-size orders.
does_not_apply_when: A SKU with no sizing or fit decision

signal.check: Return reasons show a wrong-size or wrong-fit pattern for a SKU with no dedicated sizing module on the PDP.

risk.note: The module format has no library source beyond naming sizing as a missing FUD item; verify against the brand's own return data.

prerequisites: Real size chart and fit data for the SKU
Return reasons by SKU
steps: Check return reasons for a wrong-size or wrong-fit pattern on this SKU.
Build a dedicated size or fit guide module from real measurements.
Place it near the variant selector on the PDP.
Track return rate before and after.

test.method: Compare wrong-size return rate before and after adding the guide.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Write section headings as the shopper's payoff, never a department label
hypothesis: If every heading states what the shopper gains instead of a department label like Our Ingredients, then a visitor who reads only the headings top to bottom still has a reason to buy.

signal.check: A heading reads Our Services, What Makes Us Unique, How It Works, or Our Reviews with no benefit stated.

risk.note: A copy edit.

steps: List every section heading on the page.
Rewrite each one as the payoff for the shopper, such as What's in your jar and why it works instead of Our Ingredients.
For a proof heading, use a form like Helping a real number of customers achieve an outcome.
Read only the headings top to bottom and check they sell on their own.

test.method: Run a read-only-headings test before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Score every headline on 7 traits and add an eyebrow line for a missing one
hypothesis: If a headline is scored on curiosity, pain callout, solution promise, specificity, simplicity, credibility and time frame, and hits at least 3 or 4, then it is more likely to earn attention without becoming an overloaded, unfocused line.

signal.check: A headline was shipped with no trait score, or it tries to cram in more than 1 curiosity element.

risk.note: A scoring exercise before shipping.

steps: Score the headline draft on curiosity, pain callout, solution promise, specificity, simplicity, credibility, and time frame to results.
Keep drafts scoring 3 or more.
Add an eyebrow line above the headline for a trait it is missing, instead of overloading the headline itself.
Cap curiosity at 1 element in the headline, 2 including the subhead.

test.method: Score every headline draft before choosing one to test.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Lead with the benefit family a shopper uses to pick between 2 open tabs
hypothesis: If the page leads with the benefit family the shopper actually decides on, such as saving time, earning money, pain relief, peace of mind, status, or freedom, then the spec or feature list reads as proof, not the headline.

signal.check: The page leads with a spec or feature list and buries the underlying benefit family.

risk.note: A copy reorder.

steps: Name the benefit family the shopper actually decides on: saving time, earning money, pain relief, peace of mind, status, or freedom.
For a premium good, translate the dream outcome into what the buyer feels, such as status.
Lead the page and each section with that benefit.
Move specs and features to support the benefit, not to headline it.

test.method: Compare conversion before and after reordering benefit-first.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Write every page in the customer's own words, mined from reviews and tickets
hypothesis: If page copy comes from review mining, survey answers, support tickets and sales conversations instead of the writer's own phrasing, then the copy sounds like the buyer's own thinking and lands harder.

signal.check: Page copy uses phrasing that does not appear in any review, ticket, or survey answer on file.

risk.note: A research and rewrite pass.

prerequisites: Review export, survey answers, support tickets, and any forum or ad-comment language
steps: Pull reviews, survey answers, support tickets, and forum or ad-comment language.
Highlight the exact phrases customers use to describe the problem and the win.
Rewrite key lines using those phrases instead of the writer's own words.
Check each borrowed phrase is used honestly, in context.

test.method: Compare engagement or conversion on rewritten sections against the original copy.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Make page text scannable with bullets, icons and subheads while keeping full specs available
hypothesis: If dense text is converted to bullets, icons and subheads with full specs still available, then more visitors read the key points instead of skipping the section entirely.

signal.check: A section is a dense paragraph block with no bullets, icons, or subheads.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client reported plus 25 percent CR and plus 34 percent RPV, no sample size

risk.note: A formatting change, not a content change.

steps: Find dense text blocks in the PDP description and page body.
Convert them into bullets, icons and subheads with selective bold.
Keep full specs available in a scannable form, such as an expandable section.
Leave long, engaging story leads as prose where the format calls for it.

test.method: Compare scroll-through and conversion before and after converting to scannable format.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Give every gallery image a selling point instead of just showing angles
hypothesis: If every gallery image carries a selling point, such as use, outcome, scale, or ease, then a visitor who only looks at the images still has enough to buy.

signal.check: The PDP gallery is mostly product angles with no use, outcome, or benefit images.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client reported plus 32 percent CR from gallery infographics, no sample size

risk.note: A photo and overlay production task.

prerequisites: Real product photos in use, and overlay-ready images
steps: List current gallery images and what each one shows.
Plan a mix: happy user in the outcome, product in use, scale reference, use with others, before-and-after where allowed, benefit-stat overlays.
Put text on or beside the image, not only in the page copy.
Test that a visitor who only looks at the images has enough to buy.
Never let an overlay hide the true product.

test.method: A/B test the new gallery against the current one.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Match every advertorial image to the SKU's current photo set and keep it honestly real
hypothesis: If every image on an advertorial or story page traces to the SKU's current colour, size and packaging, and every photo is honestly what it claims to be, then returns from a mismatch fall and trust holds.

signal.check: An advertorial image shows a different colour, size, or packaging than what ships today, or a generated or stock image is shown as a real customer.

risk.note: A photo audit.

prerequisites: Current SKU photo set
steps: Compare every product image on the page against the SKU's current photo set.
Replace any outdated colour, size, or packaging image.
Never present a generated or stock face as a real customer, patient, or author.
Use the real product photo wherever the product shows.

test.method: Audit page images against the current photo set before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch and after any SKU change

title: Quantify claims with a true number wherever one exists
hypothesis: If headlines, proof headings, CTAs and time claims use a true number instead of a vague word, then the claim reads more credible because it is specific and checkable.

signal.check: A claim reads trusted by happy customers or ships fast instead of a real number the brand can back.

risk.note: Only use numbers the brand record backs.

prerequisites: Substantiated claims list with real customer counts, review counts, and time-to-result figures
steps: Find every vague claim in headlines, proof headings, CTAs and time statements.
Replace each with a true number from the brand record.
Cut any claim with no matching number on file.
Recheck after every claims-list update.

test.method: Audit claims for vague-versus-specific wording before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Treat every fact in an AI-written draft as invented until matched to the brand record
hypothesis: If every name, study, number, price and testimonial in an AI draft is checked against the brand record before it ships, then the page never carries a hallucinated fact.

signal.check: An AI-assisted draft contains a name, number, study, price, or testimonial with no match in the brand record.

risk.note: A verification pass; standard before any AI-assisted copy ships.

prerequisites: Brand record with product facts, prices, and real testimonials
steps: List every name, study, number, price, and testimonial in the AI draft.
Match each one to the brand record.
Cut or rewrite anything with no match.
Treat this check as required on every AI-assisted draft, not just the first one.

test.method: Run the AI-draft verification checklist before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Keep page copy below a tenth-grade reading level
hypothesis: If page copy reads below a tenth-grade level, using concrete, short, simple words in full sentences, then more visitors understand the offer on the first read.

signal.check: A readability tool scores a page's copy at grade 10 or above, or the copy uses many staccato fragments.

risk.note: A rewrite pass.

steps: Run a readability tool on every page draft.
Rewrite anything at grade 10 or above using shorter, simpler, concrete words.
Keep full sentences; avoid repeated staccato fragments.
Re-read the copy aloud after any AI-assisted pass, since staccato tends to return.

test.method: Run a readability check before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Give a real, checkable mechanism one short name and use it everywhere on the page
hypothesis: If a product with a real mechanism gets 1 short, honest name used in the headline, subheads, body and close, then the story is easier to remember and repeat because it always points to the same idea.
does_not_apply_when: A product with no real, checkable mechanism to name

signal.check: The product has a real mechanism but the page uses 2 or more different names for it, or no name at all.

risk.note: The name must describe something real; never coin a medical-sounding name for a mechanism the product does not have.

prerequisites: The real mechanism and its evidence from the brand record
steps: Confirm the product has a real, checkable mechanism.
Generate name candidates from the form, ingredient, source, or visual of the mechanism.
Drop any overused or medical-sounding name the product cannot back.
Use the chosen name in the headline, subheads, body, and close.

test.method: Search the draft for the mechanism name and confirm only 1 name is used throughout.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Show the platform badge shoppers trust for the channel they buy on, and keep every review verifiable
hypothesis: If reviews carry a real platform badge, full name, consented photo, platform source and date, then buyers trust the proof more because it is checkable outside the brand's own control.

signal.check: Reviews show no platform source, no date, or a press logo with no quote from the outlet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client reported plus 38 percent from adding quotes under logos, no sample size

risk.note: A proof-formatting fix.

prerequisites: Review consent for names and photos
Real press quotes with permission
steps: Add the platform badge shoppers trust for the channel they buy on.
Show full name, consented photo, platform source and date on every review.
Add the outlet's actual quote under every press logo.
Avoid overusing bare or repeated featured-on logos.

test.method: A/B test adding platform badges and quotes to the proof section.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Map every testimonial to 1 named objection or belief it must answer
hypothesis: If every testimonial is chosen and placed to answer 1 named objection or install 1 needed belief, then proof does real work at the point of hesitation instead of sitting as generic praise.

signal.check: A testimonial reads as generic praise with no clear objection it answers, or several testimonials repeat the same point.

risk.note: A proof-curation task.

prerequisites: Top 5 objections ranked from research
steps: List the top 5 objections from research.
Match 1 real review to each objection, using different customer types where possible.
Place each testimonial next to the claim or section it supports, and at points of action such as under add to cart or beside the bundle selector.
Never write, edit, or invent a review to fit.

test.method: A/B test objection-matched testimonial placement against the current generic layout.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Scatter proof throughout the page instead of stacking it once
hypothesis: If proof appears above the fold, between value props, at drop-off points, near every CTA, and in a full open review grid somewhere on the page, then hesitant visitors meet proof exactly where they hesitate.

signal.check: Proof appears in only 1 block on the page, or a full review section is hidden in a carousel or accordion on mobile.

risk.note: A layout redistribution of existing proof assets.

prerequisites: A proof inventory: reviews, quotes, ratings, press mentions
steps: Inventory all available proof: reviews, ratings, quotes, press mentions.
Place proof above the fold, between value prop sections, and near every CTA.
Add a full open review grid, not a carousel, somewhere on the page.
Never hide a whole review section in a carousel or accordion on mobile.
Give video reviews a scannable headline for sound-off viewers.

test.method: A/B test scattered proof placement against a single stacked proof block.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Add phone-shot UGC and a short founder video on trust-led, high-ticket or new-brand pages
hypothesis: If a trust-led, high-ticket, or new-brand page adds phone-shot UGC and a 45-second founder video alongside written reviews, then trust rises for a category where written reviews alone are not enough.
does_not_apply_when: A low-consideration, high-volume category where written reviews already carry the proof load

signal.check: A trust-led or new-brand page has only written reviews, with no video proof and no founder appearance.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 account reported cost per lead falling from about 200 to about 30 dollars, and a page moving from about 10 percent to 15 percent, called a personal bias by its own source

risk.note: Test with and without the founder video; written reviews stay the base either way.

prerequisites: Ability to shoot phone-style UGC and a short founder video
steps: Keep written, verifiable, objection-matched reviews as the base proof.
Add 1 or more phone-shot UGC videos of the product unboxed or worn, styled like the brand's own ad.
Add a 45-second founder video for a trust-led category.
Place video below the headline, still thumbnail, no autoplay with sound.
Test the page with and without the founder video.

test.method: A/B test the page with and without video proof.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Build 3 layers of proof on a presell page: mechanism, social, and demonstration
hypothesis: If an advertorial or long sales page carries mechanism proof, social proof from 10 to 20 real quotes, and demonstration proof of the product working, then skepticism drops because 3 different kinds of evidence back the same claim.

signal.check: An advertorial has only 1 type of proof, such as reviews alone with no mechanism explanation or demonstration.

risk.note: A content-gathering and drafting task.

prerequisites: Research base with mechanism evidence and 10 to 20 real customer quotes
steps: Write mechanism proof in about 3 sentences: why the product works.
Gather 10 to 20 real quotes for social proof, including repeat-buyer reviews for consumables.
Add demonstration proof: the product visibly working.
Add specificity, such as numbers and timelines, and real third-party proof where available.
Never exaggerate a demonstration beyond what the product actually does.

test.method: Review the draft against the 3-layer checklist before launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Keep every cited study honest: real institution, real population, real result
hypothesis: If every study cited on a page keeps its real institution, population, comparison group and time frame, translated to plain numbers in code, then the brand never overstates a result it cannot defend.

signal.check: A page cites a study with no matching real institution, population, or result on file, or the study's numbers were rounded up in copy.

risk.note: Look up every study cited; never trust an AI summary of it.

prerequisites: The actual paper for every study cited
steps: List every study cited on the page.
Look up each paper directly: institution, population, design, and result.
Translate the result to a plain percentage in code, not by hand.
Cut or rewrite any citation that cannot be verified this way.

test.method: Verify every study citation before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Collect proof on purpose with a short post-purchase survey
