hypothesis: If every buyer gets a short post-purchase survey asking what motivated them and what almost stopped them, then the brand builds a growing bank of real proof and objection language instead of waiting for organic reviews.

signal.check: The brand has few usable reviews and no post-purchase survey collecting motivation and objection answers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source reported 85 to 90 percent completion, unverified

risk.note: A survey tool addition on the confirmation page.

prerequisites: A survey tool on the order confirmation page
steps: Add a post-purchase survey right after purchase asking what motivated the buy today.
Add a second question asking what concerns or doubts almost stopped the purchase.
Use open-ended questions when data is thin.
Feed answers into the proof bank and objection list.

test.method: Track survey completion and the volume of usable answers over time.
test.read_point: After 1 month of collection

title: Match the page's credibility source to who the market actually trusts
hypothesis: If the spokesperson or authority chosen for a page matches who the buyer actually trusts, rather than defaulting to a doctor, then credibility lands because the source fits the buyer's real beliefs about the category.

signal.check: A page defaults to a doctor or generic expert with no research into whether this market actually trusts that source.

risk.note: Any expert used must be real, qualified, consenting, and disclosed.

prerequisites: Research on who this market's buyers actually trust
steps: Research who the buyer trusts in this category; note if the medical system itself is distrusted in this market.
Choose a credibility source that fits that trust, not a default doctor.
Confirm any expert used is real, qualified, consenting and disclosed.
Pick a swipe or reference whose credibility source the brand actually has, if modeling structure.

test.method: Test 2 credibility choices against each other where traffic allows.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches its traffic floor

title: Show bundle and multi-pack savings in money, in the tier headline
hypothesis: If every bundle or multi-pack tier states the saving in money in its headline instead of a percentage in small text, then more shoppers pick a bigger tier because they never have to do the maths themselves.

signal.check: A bundle tier shows a percentage discount in small text instead of a money saving in the headline.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client reported plus 25 percent CR and plus 28.57 percent RPV, no sample size

risk.note: Compute the saving in code from the real price, never estimate it.

prerequisites: Real price and bundle data
steps: Compute the money saving for each tier in code from the real price data.
Show it in the tier headline, such as 3 pack, save 10 dollars.
Remove any percentage-only saving in small body text.
Match the shown saving to what the cart actually charges.

test.method: A/B test money-saving headlines against percentage-only labels.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Offer 3 bundle tiers, each with its own image and 1 honest badge on the target tier
hypothesis: If a bundle offer is cut to 3 tiers, each shown with its own image and 1 honest badge on the tier the brand wants chosen, then AOV rises because shoppers stop defaulting to the cheapest tier or leaving confused by too many options.
does_not_apply_when: A single-unit product with no multi-pack or bundle offer

signal.check: Session recordings show shoppers picking the cheapest tier or leaving the bundle selector, or the page shows more than 3 tiers with no images.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client cutting 5 tiers to 3 reported plus 53 percent CR and plus 13.5 percent AOV, no sample size, on that client's own combined changes

risk.note: Cutting a tier can hurt a real segment that wanted it; a too-attractive middle tier can cannibalise a higher-margin top tier. Model this with the offer domain first.

prerequisites: Tier sales mix and margin per tier from the offer domain
steps: Check current tier count and recordings for cheapest-tier bias or bundle-selector abandonment.
Cut to 3 tiers if more are shown.
Add 1 image per tier.
Add 1 honest badge, such as Most Popular or a real benefit badge, to the target tier only.
Model margin impact with the offer domain before shipping.

test.method: A/B test the 3-tier redesign against the current tier structure.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Keep the PDP price visible by default; only test hiding it with proof of a price objection
hypothesis: If the PDP shows the price in the buy box by default, and moving it lower is only tested where a real price objection is proven, then the store avoids losing trust from hiding a normal, expected element.
does_not_apply_when: An advertorial or presell funnel, where a different price-visibility rule applies

signal.check: The PDP price is hidden or de-emphasized with no proven price objection behind the decision.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 client with a proven price objection moved price lower and put trust above it, reporting plus 32 percent then plus 88 percent cumulative, no sample size

risk.note: Default is price visible; treat any hiding as a test, not a default.

prerequisites: Evidence of a real price objection, such as survey answers or support tickets, before testing a hidden price
steps: Keep the price visible in the buy box as the default on every PDP.
Look for evidence of a real price objection: survey answers, support tickets, or session recordings.
Only where that evidence exists, test moving the price lower with trust elements above it.
Judge the test on conversion and revenue, not on the visual change alone.

test.method: A/B test a price-position change only where a price objection is proven.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Anchor the price against a real, sourced comparison, never an invented reference price
hypothesis: If the price is anchored against a real cost of the problem, a real cost of alternatives, or a genuine sum of parts, then the offer feels fair without relying on an invented or inflated reference price.

signal.check: The page anchors price against an invented suggested retail price, a raised compare-at price, or an unsourced cost comparison.

risk.note: An invented reference price is a compliance risk, not just a weak tactic.

prerequisites: A real, sourced cost of the problem or of the closest alternatives
Current reference pricing rules for the market
steps: Find a real, sourced cost of the problem or of the closest real alternatives.
Anchor the price against that real cost, stated honestly.
Never raise a compare-at price above what was actually charged.
Check current reference pricing rules for the market before publishing.

test.method: Audit every price anchor on the page against a real source before launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Use urgency and scarcity only when it is true, and phrase it as risk, not a fake count
hypothesis: If urgency and scarcity lines use only real sale end dates, real dispatch cut-offs, and real stock levels, phrased as risk rather than an invented count, then the page keeps its persuasive edge without a compliance or trust risk.

signal.check: A countdown, low-stock count, or high-demand line has no real deadline or live stock data behind it.

risk.note: Fake urgency is banned outright; a live stock feed is worth building only where stock genuinely runs low.

prerequisites: Live stock data or a real promo calendar
steps: Check whether the sale end date, dispatch cut-off, or stock claim is real and live.
Phrase real low stock as risk, such as high demand and risk of selling out, rather than an exact fake count.
Use a countdown only for a real deadline.
Remove any urgency line with no real data behind it.

test.method: Audit every urgency and scarcity line against live data before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Present the guarantee as confidence, matched word for word to policy, beside every buy CTA
hypothesis: If the guarantee is stated as 1 clear, confident policy that matches the brand's real terms exactly, and repeated beside every buy CTA, then hesitant buyers get consistent reassurance instead of a confusing mix of guarantee wording.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with no guarantee and no operational ability to carry one, where the slot is used for proof instead

signal.check: The guarantee is worded differently in 2 or more places on the page, or does not match the real policy.

risk.note: A copy consistency fix.

prerequisites: Real guarantee and refund policy from the brand record
steps: Pull the brand's real guarantee terms.
Write 1 clear guarantee statement that matches those terms exactly.
Use that same wording beside every buy CTA on the page.
If no guarantee exists, use that slot for proof instead.

test.method: Compare guarantee wording across the page before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Only claim exclusivity, such as not sold on Amazon, after checking it live
hypothesis: If an exclusivity claim is checked against live marketplace listings before it ships, then the brand never states an exclusivity claim a buyer can disprove with 1 search.

signal.check: The page claims the product is not sold elsewhere with no recent check of live marketplace listings.

risk.note: A quick web check before shipping the claim.

prerequisites: A live check of marketplace listings for the product
steps: Search major marketplaces for the product before making an exclusivity claim.
Ship the claim only if the product is genuinely not listed there.
Re-check the claim on a schedule, since marketplace listings change.
Remove the claim immediately if a listing appears.

test.method: Re-check marketplace listings on a set schedule.
test.read_point: Monthly, and before every relaunch of the claim

title: Close long pages with 2 honest options: leave and keep the problem, or try it risk-free
hypothesis: If the closer gives the reader 2 clear options, leaving with the problem or trying the offer under the real guarantee, then the choice feels honest and the guarantee gets one more moment of visibility before the reader leaves.

signal.check: The page's close has no clear restated choice, guarantee, or discount, and just ends.

risk.note: A copy addition.

prerequisites: Real guarantee and discount terms
steps: Write the close as 2 options: leave and keep the problem, or try the offer under the real guarantee.
Restate the discount and guarantee beside the last CTA.
Never add a page-only price scarcity line in the close unless it is enforced.

test.method: A/B test adding the two-options close.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Build a real-time low-stock display wired to live inventory for a SKU genuinely close to selling out
hypothesis: If a low-stock display reads live inventory instead of a static or randomised count, then urgency copy stays honest and still moves hesitant buyers on the SKUs that are actually running low.
does_not_apply_when: A SKU with plenty of stock, where a low-stock display would be false

signal.check: A SKU is genuinely close to selling out but the page has no live stock indicator, or an existing indicator is static or randomised.

risk.note: Never fake this display; wire it to real inventory data only.

prerequisites: Live inventory data the page can read
steps: Identify SKUs with real, live stock data showing they are genuinely close to selling out.
Build a low-stock display that reads live inventory, never a static or randomised number.
Show it only for SKUs where it is true.
Remove the display automatically once stock rises.

test.method: Compare conversion on genuinely low-stock SKUs with and without the live display.
test.read_point: After enough low-stock events to compare

title: Strip navigation to logo, cart and 1 CTA on single-offer campaign and advertorial pages
hypothesis: If a single-offer campaign page, advertorial, or quiz result page removes the full site navigation down to a logo, 1 CTA, and required policy links, then fewer paid visitors leak away to browse instead of converting.
does_not_apply_when: Storefront PDPs, collections and the homepage, which need a browse-friendly nav instead

signal.check: A dedicated campaign page fed only by paid traffic still shows the full site navigation and outbound links.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 audited site showed navigation taking about 33.2 percent of clicks

risk.note: Test nav removal on campaign traffic only, never as a storefront default.

prerequisites: Area map or click-share data for the page's navigation, if available
steps: Confirm the page is a single-offer campaign, advertorial, or quiz result page fed only by paid traffic.
Strip the navigation to logo, 1 CTA, and required policy links in a small footer.
Remove outbound links inside testimonials and linked logos; anchor proof on-page instead.
Keep this stripped nav only on dedicated pages, never on the storefront.

test.method: A/B test the stripped navigation against the full site nav on campaign traffic.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Cut storefront navigation to 7 items or fewer, kept visual, with Shop always exposed
hypothesis: If storefront PDPs, collections and the homepage cut navigation to 7 items or fewer, drop near-zero-click items, and keep Shop exposed, then browsing visitors find products faster without losing access to policy pages.
does_not_apply_when: A single-offer campaign page, which strips navigation entirely instead

signal.check: The storefront nav has more than 7 top-level items, includes a redundant Home link, or buries the Shop menu.

risk.note: Move FAQ out of the nav only after its answers live on the PDP.

prerequisites: Nav click share per item, from an area map
steps: Pull nav click share per item.
Remove items near 0 percent of clicks, and remove the redundant Home link since the logo goes home.
Move About, Contact, Blog and FAQ to a sub-menu or footer in smaller text, keeping FAQ only if its answers also live on the PDP.
Use a nested menu for a large catalogue, with no extra click to reach the shop.

test.method: Compare View Product Rate and click share before and after the nav trim.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Open a cart drawer on add to cart instead of reloading the page
hypothesis: If add to cart opens a lightweight drawer with the basics, a higher-tier option, and a few minor cross-sells instead of reloading the page, then fewer shoppers lose momentum after adding a product.

signal.check: Add to cart triggers a full page reload, or the cart is stacked with so many widgets it screams at once.

risk.note: Verify the theme's cart drawer support before building.

prerequisites: Theme or platform support for a cart drawer, verified in the UI
Margin modeled for any free-shipping or discount progress bar
steps: Confirm the theme or platform supports a cart drawer.
Build the drawer to open on add to cart with no page reload.
Include items, a higher-tier option, a few minor cross-sells, and an honest free-shipping or discount progress bar.
Model the progress bar's margin impact with the offer domain first.
Strip the drawer down if it starts to feel cluttered.

test.method: Compare cart-to-checkout conversion before and after the drawer.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Fire pop-ups only on intent signals, never in the first 3 to 5 seconds
hypothesis: If discount and email pop-ups fire only on exit intent, right after add to cart for shoppers who have not checked out, or at the scroll depth where drop-off happens, then fewer visitors are annoyed before they have seen anything worth reacting to.

signal.check: A pop-up fires within the first 3 to 5 seconds of a page load.

risk.note: Mobile exit-intent needs a different trigger than a desktop mouse-leave event; verify in the tool.

prerequisites: Scroll-depth data for the page, and margin data for any discount offered
steps: Remove any pop-up trigger set to fire on page load or within the first 3 to 5 seconds.
Set triggers to exit intent, post-add-to-cart for shoppers who have not checked out, or the scroll depth where the heatmap shows drop-off.
Check the mobile-safe version of the exit-intent trigger in the tool.
Judge the pop-up on sales, not pop-up view count.

test.method: Compare sales and email capture before and after retiming the pop-up.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Fix or remove false affordances and near-zero-click dead controls
hypothesis: If elements styled like buttons that go nowhere are made into real links or made to look inert, and controls under about 1 percent of clicks are removed unless they prevent a costly problem, then fewer visitors rage-click or get confused by fake interactivity.

signal.check: An area map shows a styled element with near-zero clicks that looks clickable but is not, or a genuinely dead control under about 1 percent of clicks with no clear value.

risk.note: Low click share does not always mean low value; keep size charts, returns, and support links even if rarely clicked.

prerequisites: An area map or click-share report for the page
steps: Pull the area map and list elements with near-zero click share.
For anything styled like a button that goes nowhere, make it a real internal link or make it look inert.
Remove a genuinely dead control under about 1 percent of clicks, unless it prevents a costly problem such as a size chart or a returns link.
Re-check rage clicks after the change.

test.method: Compare rage-click rate before and after fixing or removing dead controls.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 weeks of traffic

title: Build and review every page mobile first, using the brand's own device split
hypothesis: If every page is built and reviewed on mobile before desktop, using the brand's own real device split, then the majority device gets the best version instead of a shrunk-down afterthought.

signal.check: A page was designed and reviewed on desktop first, with mobile treated as a shrink-to-fit pass.

risk.note: A process change, not a code change.

prerequisites: The brand's own device split by page, from analytics
steps: Pull the brand's own device split for this page from analytics.
Design and review the page on mobile first.
Read scroll maps on mobile before desktop.
Use the brand's real split, not a generic industry number, to prioritise effort.

test.method: Compare conversion by device before and after adopting a mobile-first build process.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Pin the PDP CTA on mobile with live price, without covering the size or shade selector
hypothesis: If the PDP's pinned mobile CTA shows the live price and saving, updates on variant tap, and never covers the size or shade selector, then shoppers always have a working buy path without being forced past a required choice.

signal.check: The pinned CTA scrolls away, covers a required selector, or does not update when the variant changes.

risk.note: A sticky-element build; test that it never blocks a required choice.

prerequisites: Theme or platform support for a pinned CTA, verified in the UI
steps: Add a pinned CTA on the PDP mobile view.
Show live price and any saving, updating on variant tap.
Confirm it never covers the size or shade selector.
On a story-led advertorial, trigger the sticky button only at the product reveal instead of from the top.

test.method: Compare add-to-cart rate before and after adding or fixing the pinned CTA.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Never hide reviews or other critical content behind a carousel, accordion, or tab on mobile
hypothesis: If reviews and other critical content stay open on mobile instead of hidden behind a carousel, accordion, or tab, then more visitors actually see the proof and information that would move them to buy.
does_not_apply_when: SEO text on a page that must rank, which may stay in an accordion for length

signal.check: A full review section, key spec, or other critical content is hidden behind a swipeable carousel or a closed accordion on mobile.

risk.note: A layout fix; low cost.

steps: Audit the mobile page for content hidden in a carousel, accordion, or tab.
Open reviews and other critical content by default on mobile.
Leave only non-critical SEO text in an accordion where length requires it.
Re-check after any theme or template update.

test.method: Compare engagement and conversion before and after exposing hidden content.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Shrink mobile chrome so no oversized logo or announcement bar buries the headline
hypothesis: If the mobile logo and any announcement bar are sized down, then the headline and CTA fit in the first mobile screen instead of being pushed below it.

signal.check: An oversized logo or announcement bar pushes the headline and CTA below the first mobile screen.

risk.note: A sizing fix in the theme.

steps: Measure how much vertical space the logo and announcement bar take on mobile.
Shrink both until the headline and CTA fit in the first screen.
Re-check on every device preset.

test.method: Compare the mobile fold before and after shrinking the chrome.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Cut mobile forms to 4 fields or fewer with visible labels
hypothesis: If mobile lead and quiz-capture forms use visible labels, 1 full-name field, and 4 fields or fewer, then completion rate rises because the form is faster and clearer to fill one-handed.

signal.check: A mobile form uses placeholder text as the only label, has more than 4 fields, or splits the name into 2 fields with no need.

risk.note: A form redesign; low cost.

steps: Count the current form's fields and label style.
Move any placeholder-only label to a separate, always-visible label.
Cut to 4 fields or fewer, using 1 full-name field.
Add progressive disclosure where the form tool allows it.

test.method: Compare form completion rate before and after the redesign.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Check every screen width in the browser's responsive mode before sending traffic
hypothesis: If every page is checked across every common device width, including a slow drag between presets, before traffic starts, then broken layouts and overflow issues are caught before they cost a sale.

signal.check: A page was never checked in responsive mode across multiple widths before launch.

risk.note: A QA step, not a design change.

steps: Open the page in the browser's responsive mode.
Check every common device preset and slow-drag between widths.
Check tap targets, overflow, and the pinned CTA at each width.
Fix any break before sending traffic.

test.method: Run this check before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Treat page weight as a conversion problem and fix it before launch
hypothesis: If heavy images, video, and unused widgets are cut or deferred before a page goes live, then load time drops and fewer visitors leave before the page finishes loading.

signal.check: A page's speed test shows a mobile load time at or above 2 seconds, or unused builder widgets are still loaded.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 unnamed study reported a load-time curve with a hard drop past 1 to 2 seconds, uncited

risk.note: Hand the report to the speed domain if the target is missed.

prerequisites: A speed test run on the page, throttled to mobile
steps: Run a speed test on the page, throttled to mobile.
Compress images, defer scripts, and remove unused builder widgets.
Target under 2 seconds on mobile and never over 4.
Hand a report to the speed domain if the target is still missed after these fixes.

test.method: Re-run the speed test after each round of fixes.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Set page length by traffic warmth and SKU tier, not a fixed word count
hypothesis: If cold, unaware traffic on a hero SKU gets a long page with many value-prop and proof sections, and warm traffic on a long ad or search gets a short page with the offer up front, then length matches what the visitor actually needs instead of a house style.

signal.check: Every product on a catalogue store uses the same page length regardless of traffic warmth or SKU tier.

risk.note: A structural decision recorded in the brief, tested where scroll data disagrees.

prerequisites: Traffic warmth and SKU tier known per page
steps: Classify each page's traffic as cold, unaware, or problem-aware versus warm, solution-aware, or most-aware.
Classify the SKU as hero, core, or tail for a catalogue brand.
Set a long page with many value-prop and proof sections for cold, hero-SKU traffic.
Set a short page with the offer near the top for warm traffic or a tail SKU.
Write the length decision and its reason in the page brief.
Propose a length test only where scroll data disagrees with the choice.

test.method: Compare scroll depth and conversion against the length decision recorded in the brief.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Cut any section that does not move the visitor 1 step closer to buying
hypothesis: If every section is checked against whether it moves the visitor 1 step closer to the purchase, and any that do not are cut, then the page reads as a persuasion machine instead of a checklist of boilerplate sections.

signal.check: A section exists on the page with no clear job in moving the visitor toward the purchase.

risk.note: A pruning pass; reversible.

steps: List every section on the page.
Ask what step it moves the visitor toward: awareness, desire, trust, or the buy decision.
Cut any section with no clear answer.
Re-check after adding any new section in the future.

test.method: Audit the page section by section before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Repeat the core 3 to 5 pains and desires deliberately on cold long-form pages only
hypothesis: If a cold, long-form page deliberately repeats its core 3 to 5 pains and desires in different forms, such as a list, a story beat, and a question, while a short or premium page avoids repeating them, then the repetition reinforces rather than annoys, because it matches the format it appears in.
does_not_apply_when: A short or premium-brand page, where repetition reads as pushy

signal.check: A cold long-form page states its core pains only once, or a short premium page repeats them several times.

risk.note: Bounded by the brand voice rule on agitation; do not let repetition become pushy.

prerequisites: Brand voice rules and limits on agitation
The core 3 to 5 pains and desires from research
steps: Confirm the page is cold traffic and long-form.
Identify the core 3 to 5 pains and desires from research.
Repeat them in different forms across the page: a list, a story beat, a question.
For a short or premium page, state each pain or desire once only.
Check the brand voice rule before finalising the repetition level.

test.method: A/B test a repetition-heavy version against a single-mention version on cold long-form traffic.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Gather a full research base before drafting any advertorial
hypothesis: If an advertorial draft starts only after current state, desired state, top pains and desires, failed alternatives, objections, mechanism evidence, and 10 to 20 real review quotes are written down, then the draft rests on real buyer language instead of a guess.

signal.check: A team is about to draft an advertorial with no written research base covering pains, alternatives, objections and the mechanism.

risk.note: A research and documentation task.

prerequisites: Reviews, tickets, ad comments, and sales-call notes available to mine
steps: Gather current state, pains and daily frustrations, and desired state, goals and moments they want back.
Rank the 3 to 5 biggest pains and desires.
List every alternative tried and why it failed, including doing nothing.
List the top 5 objections.
Write the real root cause and mechanism with its evidence.
Gather 10 to 20 real review quotes and define the persona.
Hold this base in a shared document before drafting begins.

test.method: Compare draft revision count and reviewer flags for advertorials built with and without a full research base.
test.read_point: After the first 5 advertorials tracked this way

title: Rank candidate pains by urgency, scale and relevance, and consider an under-served sub-avatar
hypothesis: If candidate pains are ranked on urgency, scale and relevance before choosing which to lead with, and a crowded niche picks an under-served sub-avatar instead of the category's top pain, then the lead pain reaches a real, reachable segment instead of copying every competitor's angle.

signal.check: The advertorial's lead pain was picked by habit or by copying the category leader, with no ranking against urgency, scale, and relevance.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 account reported cutting CPM to about 20 dollars by targeting an under-served sub-avatar, 1 account, no test

risk.note: A prioritisation exercise before drafting.

prerequisites: A ranked list of candidate pains from research
steps: List every candidate pain from research.
Score each on urgency, scale, and relevance.
Lead with the top-ranked pain; fold smaller urgent pains in as secondary benefits.
In a crowded niche, consider an under-served sub-avatar instead of the category's most obvious pain.

test.method: Compare CPM and conversion across 2 pain-led angles for the same product.
test.read_point: After each angle reaches a comparable spend

title: Test the advertorial's big idea against the competitor test before drafting
hypothesis: If the 1-line angle is checked against whether a competitor could say the same thing, and rewritten when it fails that test, then the advertorial's core idea is genuinely differentiated instead of a generic category claim.

signal.check: The chosen 1-line angle could be said by any competitor in the category with no change.

risk.note: A quick check before drafting proceeds.

steps: Write the 1-line big idea where product uniqueness, the market's live debate, and the chosen prospect overlap.
Ask if a competitor could say this same line.
If yes, return to the pain-ranking step and try again.
Give every product component a truthful reason: why this form, this source, this dose.

test.method: Run the competitor test on every new angle before drafting.
test.read_point: Before drafting begins

title: Name the mechanism honestly, with a simple, checkable causal chain
hypothesis: If the mechanism is named with the product's own real words, mapped 1 to 1 to the root cause with as few causal steps as possible, then the story stays inside what the product can actually prove.

signal.check: The mechanism claim has more than 1 or 2 causal steps, uses a metaphor that does not match the real action, or names a mechanism the product does not have.

risk.note: An invented mechanism is a compliance risk, not just weak copy.

prerequisites: The real mechanism and its evidence from the brand record
steps: Write the mechanism using the product's own ingredient or component words.
Map it 1 to 1 to the root cause.
Cut causal steps until as few as possible remain.
Check the metaphor used matches the mechanism's real action.
Only claim only this combination works when it is true.

test.method: Ask a reader to retell the mechanism in 1 or 2 lines; if they cannot, simplify further.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Commit every advertorial to 1 editorial frame and hold it to the end
hypothesis: If an advertorial commits to 1 frame, such as breaking news, David versus Goliath, or a buyer's guide, and holds it through every section, then the page reads as a consistent piece instead of drifting into a plain sales letter.

signal.check: The advertorial mixes 2 or more frames, or a Warning frame does not warn about anything specific.

risk.note: A structural check on the draft.

prerequisites: The buyer's main obstacle named from research
steps: Pick 1 frame: breaking news, authority breakdown, David versus Goliath, warning, scandal, social proof, origin discovery, comparison, local or relatable, or scarcity.
Name the frame in 1 word and confirm it can be held to the end.
Cut any bolted-on clause that does not fit the frame.
Rebuild the draft if it reads like a plain sales letter instead of the chosen frame.

test.method: Name the frame in 1 word after drafting and check it held throughout.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Order the advertorial in the proven 14-block sequence, adapting only the lead and reveal point
hypothesis: If an advertorial follows the merged block order, disclosure, headline, lead, agitation, why nothing else worked, root cause, mechanism, proof, objections, offer, CTA, late proof, close, sign-off, then the page covers every persuasion job in a tested sequence.

signal.check: An advertorial draft skips 1 or more of the standard blocks, or places the offer or proof in an unusual spot with no stated reason.

risk.note: The draft is a document; nothing publishes until it passes review and QA.

prerequisites: Research base and chosen frame completed
Lead length decided from the feeding ad
steps: Start with the disclosure label and any true urgency bar.
Write the headline in the chosen frame with a subhead adding the mechanism or a proof stat.
Write the lead, adapting its length to the feeding ad, then agitation and why-nothing-else-worked.
Write the root cause reframe, then the mechanism and product reveal with the first CTA soon after.
Write the proof stack, then the objections block.
Write the offer, price context, and guarantee, then the remaining CTAs.
Close with late proof, the two-options close, an honest sign-off, and the disclosure again.

test.method: Check the draft against the block order before review.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Write a why-nothing-else-worked block naming every real alternative honestly
hypothesis: If the advertorial names every real alternative the buyer tried, including doing nothing, with an honest limit for each, then the reframe to the product's mechanism feels earned instead of skipped.

signal.check: The advertorial jumps straight from agitation to the mechanism with no honest accounting of what the buyer already tried.

risk.note: No unsupported claim that a competitor or alternative fails; every limit stated must be accurate.

prerequisites: Research on real alternatives buyers try and why they fail
steps: List every real alternative the buyer tries, including doing nothing and the expert or professional path.
Write 1 honest limit for each alternative.
Never claim a competitor or alternative fails with no support.
Place this block after agitation and before the root-cause reframe.

test.method: Check every claimed limit against real evidence before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Write a dedicated objections block covering risk, price, time, safety and authority
hypothesis: If a dedicated block answers risk, price, time, safety and authority objections, such as why hasn't my doctor told me, before the offer appears, then fewer readers reach the CTA still holding an unanswered doubt.

signal.check: An advertorial has no dedicated objections block, leaving risk, price, time, safety or authority doubts unanswered before the offer.

risk.note: A content addition before the offer block.

prerequisites: Top 5 objections ranked from research
steps: Pull the top 5 objections from research: risk, price, time, safety, and authority doubts.
Write 1 honest answer to each.
Place this block before the offer and guarantee block.
Keep an FAQ afterward only for objections that skim-readers still reach.

test.method: A/B test adding the dedicated objections block.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Space about 4 CTAs across a long advertorial, or use 1 floating CTA
hypothesis: If a long advertorial places about 4 CTAs, after the hook, after the mechanism, after the proof, and after the objections, or uses 1 floating CTA instead, then a reader ready to buy at any point always has a nearby way to act.

signal.check: A long advertorial has only 1 CTA at the very bottom of the page.

risk.note: A layout and copy addition.

steps: Identify 4 natural CTA points: after the hook, after the mechanism reveal, after the proof stack, and after the objections block.
Add a CTA at each point, or build 1 floating CTA that follows the reader instead.
Vary the CTA wording slightly by section rather than repeating the same line.
Test CTA style only once traffic supports it.

test.method: A/B test 4 spaced CTAs against a single bottom CTA.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Test the hook and headline hardest before any other advertorial element
hypothesis: If format, then headline, then first-proof-block position, then CTA style are tested in that order, then the highest-leverage elements get tested first and CTA-style tests wait until traffic genuinely supports them.

signal.check: A CTA-style test is running before the format and headline have been tested, or on a page with far less traffic than the source requires.

risk.note: A test-sequencing decision, handed to the testing domain to size.

prerequisites: Weekly sessions and orders for the page
steps: Test the page format first.
Test the headline next.
Test the position of the first proof block third.
Test CTA style last, only with traffic in the thousands of visitors a day.

test.method: Track which test is running against this priority order.
test.read_point: Ongoing, reviewed each test cycle

title: Keep the story continuous; audit for the sentence where it turns into a pitch
hypothesis: If every sentence where the story turns into a sales pitch is found and rewritten as a story event, then the reader never feels sold to at the product reveal, which should reduce mid-page drop-off.

signal.check: A story-frame advertorial has a clear point where narrative stops and feature-and-price copy begins.

risk.note: A copy-editing pass.

steps: Read the draft and mark every sentence where story shifts to a sales pitch.
Rewrite each marked sentence as a story event instead of a pitch line.
Only use a device like my doctor asked where to get it if a real person said it.
Re-read to confirm the reader would not feel sold to at the reveal.

test.method: Run the story-stop audit before every launch of a story-frame advertorial.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Write the after-state first in a transformation story, then build the before-state backwards
hypothesis: If a transformation story is drafted by writing the after-state first and building the before-state backwards, then the reader ends with real hope for a problem they have had for years, instead of a story that just lists features.
does_not_apply_when: A page with no personal transformation story to tell

signal.check: A transformation story was drafted linearly from before to after with no separate after-state-first pass.

risk.note: A drafting technique.

steps: Write the after-state first: what the reader's life looks like once the problem is solved.
Build the before-state backwards from that after-state, spending real length there.
Use the life-shrinking ladder to build the before-state's tension.
End the story with real hope, not a feature recap.

test.method: Compare reader completion rate for the after-state-first drafting method against a linear draft.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Write subheads that stand alone and tell the story in order when read by themselves
hypothesis: If every subhead in an advertorial makes sense on its own and the full set of subheads tells the story in order, then a reader who only skims the subheads still gets the full arc and is more likely to slow down and read.

signal.check: Reading only the subheads in order does not tell a coherent story, or a subhead makes no sense out of context.

risk.note: A copy-editing pass.

steps: Pull every subhead out of the draft in order.
Read them as a standalone list and check they tell the story.
Rewrite any subhead that only makes sense with its paragraph attached.
Repeat the paragraph's image right after its matching subhead.

test.method: Run the subheads-only read test before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Model a swipe's structure and pacing only, never its content, and pick one the brand can back
hypothesis: If a swipe file is used only for section order and pacing, and the brand picks a swipe whose credibility source it actually has, then the draft benefits from a proven skeleton without copying claims or a credibility the brand cannot back.

signal.check: A swipe file's exact wording, claims, or images appear in the draft, or the swipe's credibility source does not match the brand's own.

risk.note: Structure only; content always comes from the brand's own facts.

prerequisites: A folder of swipe files from ad libraries and sponsored placements
steps: Find swipes in ad libraries, sponsored placements, or affiliate hubs, in and out of niche.
Pick a swipe whose credibility source the brand genuinely has.
Instruct any AI tool to follow the section order and pacing only, writing all copy from the brand's own facts.
Check the final draft for any copied wording, claim, or image.

test.method: Compare the final draft against the swipe for copied content before every launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Cut every quiz question that has no clear job
hypothesis: If every quiz question either changes the recommendation, gives research the team will read, builds micro-commitment, seeds a belief, or pre-handles a real objection, then the quiz stays as short as it can be while still doing real work.

signal.check: A quiz question exists with no stated job in changing the recommendation, seeding a belief, or handling an objection.

risk.note: A quiz content audit.

prerequisites: The beliefs the buyer must hold, and the top objections, listed
steps: List the beliefs the buyer must hold and the top objections.
Label every existing or planned question: recommend, research, commit, seed, or pre-handle.
Cut any question with no label.
Re-check the labels whenever a question is added or changed.

test.method: Compare quiz completion rate before and after cutting unlabeled questions.
test.read_point: After the quiz reaches about 100 submissions

title: Test the quiz's first 3 questions before anything else, judged with downstream purchase
hypothesis: If the first 3 quiz questions are tested first, and judged on both throughput past question 3 and downstream purchase rate, then a quiz variant that lets more starters through without lowering purchase rate can be found before investing in the rest of the quiz.

signal.check: The quiz's later questions or results page were tested and rebuilt before the first 3 questions were ever tested.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 illustration showed 70 percent versus 85 percent passing question 3, not a measured result

risk.note: Judge on downstream purchase, since letting more low-intent takers through can lower purchase rate even as completion rises.

prerequisites: Per-question drop-off tracking on the quiz
steps: Track the share of quiz starters who pass question 3.
Test 2 versions of the first 3 questions.
Judge the winner on downstream purchase rate and RPV, not just throughput.
Only then move on to testing later questions.

test.method: A/B test 2 versions of the first 3 questions.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches about 100 submissions

title: Open the quiz with the least invasive, most important question
hypothesis: If the quiz opens with the least invasive, most important question, usually the main goal, and puts personal or demographic questions later unless they change the recommendation, then fewer visitors drop out at question 1.

signal.check: The quiz opens with an age, weight, or health question with no clear reason it changes the recommendation.

risk.note: A question-order change.

steps: Identify the main-goal question as the likely opener.
Check whether any demographic question genuinely changes the recommendation.
Move any demographic question that does not change the recommendation later in the quiz.
Open with the least invasive, most important question.

test.method: Compare question-1 drop-off before and after reordering.
test.read_point: After the quiz reaches about 100 submissions

title: Rotate quiz input types and avoid typed input at launch
hypothesis: If the quiz rotates input types, no more than 2 or 3 of the same format in a row, and avoids typed input at launch, then fewer visitors get bored or stuck on a form field.

signal.check: The quiz uses the same input format, such as single choice, for more than 3 questions in a row, or asks for typed input at launch.

risk.note: A format-variety fix.

steps: List the input type for every quiz question.
Rotate formats so no more than 2 or 3 of the same type appear in a row.
Avoid typed input at launch; use numeric input only where a number drives the result.
Give visible tap feedback without heavy effects.

test.method: Compare per-question drop-off before and after rotating input types.
test.read_point: After the quiz reaches about 100 submissions

title: Insert a real info or nurture screen about every 3 to 5 quiz questions
hypothesis: If an info or nurture screen with real value, such as how the method works or a normalising message, appears about every 3 to 5 questions, then longer quizzes keep visitors engaged instead of feeling like an endless form.
does_not_apply_when: A quiz shorter than about 6 questions, which may not need a nurture screen

signal.check: A quiz longer than 6 questions has no info or nurture screens, or any percentage or projection shown has no real measured base.

risk.note: Any percentage comparison must come from a real measured base; any loading or projection screen must be a real calculation.

prerequisites: Real data for any percentage or projection shown on a nurture screen
steps: Plan an info or nurture screen about every 3 to 5 questions for quizzes longer than about 6 questions.
Write content that reflects the answers so far: how the method works, real authority, or real social proof.
Add a normalising screen after a failure-type question.
Check every percentage, graph, or loading screen uses a real measured base or a real calculation, never a simulated one.

test.method: Compare completion rate before and after adding nurture screens.
test.read_point: After the quiz reaches about 100 submissions

title: Start quiz length at 8 to 12 questions and add length only when nurture screens carry real education
hypothesis: If a product quiz starts at 8 to 12 questions and only grows longer when the category is problem-solution and nurture screens carry real education, then the quiz stays as short as the category allows without cutting a question that genuinely earns its place.

signal.check: A quiz runs well beyond 12 questions with no nurture screens, or a simple product-recommendation quiz has grown long with no added job per question.

risk.note: 3 sources disagree on the right length; test a shorter version against the current one.

steps: Start a new quiz at 8 to 12 questions.
Add length only when the category is problem-solution and each added question has a stated job.
Add nurture screens to carry education if the quiz grows past about 12 questions.
Test a shorter version against a longer one on completion and downstream purchase.

test.method: A/B test a shorter quiz against a longer one.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches about 100 submissions

title: Ask what the buyer already tried and use it for both the recommendation and the awareness stage
hypothesis: If the quiz asks what the buyer already tried and what routine is realistic, then the brand can both recommend the right product and read the buyer's awareness stage from the answer, mostly-tried-nothing meaning top-of-funnel and named failed products meaning further along.

signal.check: The quiz has no question about what the buyer already tried, so awareness stage and past effort are both guessed.

risk.note: A question addition.

steps: Add a question asking what the buyer has already tried and what routine is realistic for them.
Use the answer to inform the product or bundle recommendation.
Read the awareness stage from the answer: mostly untried means top-of-funnel, named failed products mean further along.
Feed this signal into the page copy and follow-up email.

test.method: Compare recommendation accuracy and downstream purchase with and without this question.
test.read_point: After the quiz reaches about 100 submissions

title: Build the quiz results page to show the buyer's own answers, the rule, and 1 clear buy button
hypothesis: If the results page shows the shopper's own answers, the rule that links them to the recommended SKU, then product details, price, real reviews, delivery and returns, and 1 buy button with no exits, then trust and conversion both rise because the recommendation feels earned and the path to buy is clear.

signal.check: The results page has no visible link between the answers and the recommendation, shows exits at the buy box, or uses a timer with no real deadline.

risk.note: Personalisation must be real; never show the same SKU for every answer while claiming a match.

prerequisites: The rule that maps answers to a SKU, size, or bundle
steps: Show the shopper's own answers back to them.
State the rule that links those answers to the recommended SKU, size, or bundle.
Let the shopper correct a consumption or preference assumption.
Add product details, price, real reviews, delivery and returns, and 1 buy button.
Remove exits at the buy box, and use a timer only for a real deadline.

test.method: A/B test the results page against a version with no visible answer-to-recommendation link.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Route each quiz answer to its matching page or offer, and export answers on a fixed schedule
hypothesis: If quiz answers route to a matching page and offer where one exists, feed the email platform, and get exported and reported at least twice a month, then the quiz drives both better-matched sales and a growing research asset the team actually reads.

signal.check: Quiz answers are collected but never exported or reviewed, or every answer routes to the same generic page regardless of the response.

risk.note: Requires the quiz tool and email platform to share field mapping.

prerequisites: Email platform field mapping for quiz answers
A page and offer per pain point, where they exist
steps: Map each answer or answer combination to a matching page and offer where one exists.
Pass answers to the email platform for branching the follow-up sequence.
Export the full answer set and report at about 100 submissions, then at least twice a month.
Turn the most-picked pains into candidate ad angles.

test.method: Track routed-page conversion against the generic page's conversion.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Decide the quiz email gate by KPI, and always separate marketing consent
hypothesis: If the decision to gate the quiz result behind an email is made by comparing front-end conversion against list growth, with marketing consent always a separate choice, then the brand picks the trade-off deliberately instead of copying a default.

signal.check: The quiz gates the result behind an email with no comparison against an ungated version, or bundles marketing consent with the email capture itself.

risk.note: Test gated versus ungated rather than assuming one is right.

prerequisites: Current front-end conversion rate and list growth rate
steps: Compare front-end conversion and cash impact of gating against list growth value.
For a subscription offer with a real email program, lean toward gating.
For a one-off product judged on front-end revenue, make email optional or place it after the recommendation.
Always take marketing consent as its own separate choice, explaining what will be sent.

test.method: A/B test gated versus ungated quiz results on purchase rate and RPV.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches about 100 submissions

title: Judge every quiz on completion rate and downstream purchase together, never completion alone
hypothesis: If a quiz's success is judged by completion rate and the purchase rate and RPV that follow, compared against direct-to-PDP on the same traffic, then a quiz that only looks good on completion but hurts purchase rate gets caught before it scales.

signal.check: A quiz's reporting shows only completion rate, with no downstream purchase or RPV comparison against direct-to-PDP.

risk.note: A reporting discipline, not a page change.

prerequisites: Quiz-path and direct-to-PDP purchase data on the same traffic
steps: Define completion as completers over starters.
Expect roughly 1 percent drop per question and look for any spike question.
Compare quiz-path purchase rate and RPV against direct-to-PDP on the same traffic.
Report both completion and downstream purchase together, never completion alone.

test.method: Build a standing report comparing quiz-path and direct-to-PDP purchase rate.
test.read_point: Monthly

title: Draft the quiz with AI from the research base, then review every question's job and every claim
hypothesis: If the quiz is drafted with AI from the written research base, not from the founder's belief or a swiped quiz, and every question's job and every claim is reviewed afterward, then the draft moves faster without shipping an unlabeled question or an invented statistic.

signal.check: A quiz draft was written from a founder's opinion or a competitor's swiped quiz, with no research base behind it, or no review pass for question jobs and claims.

risk.note: A process discipline for the drafting stage.

prerequisites: The written research base
steps: Feed the AI tool the written research base, not a founder's opinion or a competitor's quiz.
Draft the quiz questions, info screens, and results page copy.
Review every question against its labeled job.
Review every claim, percentage, or projection for a real, measured base before shipping.

test.method: Track review-pass findings across drafts to see if issues decrease over time.
test.read_point: After each new quiz draft

title: Never pre-select a subscription option in a quiz or checkout flow
hypothesis: If a subscription option is never pre-ticked in a quiz result or checkout flow, and the shopper must actively choose it, then the brand avoids a consent violation and the subscription rate reflects real demand.

signal.check: A quiz result or checkout screen has a subscription option pre-selected with no clear opt-in from the shopper.

risk.note: Pre-selected subscription is a consent risk in many markets; check current rules.

prerequisites: Current consent rules for subscription pre-selection in the market
steps: Audit every quiz result and checkout screen for a pre-ticked subscription option.
Set the default to unchecked, requiring an active choice.
Check current market rules on subscription pre-selection and auto-renew consent.
Re-check after any checkout or quiz-tool update.

test.method: Audit checkout and quiz screens before every launch and after every tool update.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Judge every funnel step by contribution per buyer, not take rate
hypothesis: If a direct-response funnel is judged by contribution per buyer at each step instead of raw take rate, then the team optimises for real profit instead of a vanity conversion number on a low-margin add-on.

signal.check: A funnel step, such as an order bump or OTO, is reported only by take rate with no contribution-per-buyer figure alongside it.

risk.note: A reporting change, not a page change.

prerequisites: COGS per SKU from finance
steps: Pull COGS and contribution per SKU from finance.
Compute contribution per buyer for the sales page, order page, and every OTO.
Report contribution per buyer alongside take rate for every funnel step.
Judge test wins on contribution, not take rate alone.

test.method: Compare decisions made under contribution-per-buyer reporting against the prior take-rate-only reporting.
test.read_point: After a full business cycle

title: Build the sales page with its 8 must-haves, from a scored headline to market credibility
hypothesis: If an outcome-led sales page includes a scored headline, real urgency, real scarcity, a risk-reversal guarantee, the mechanism, objection-matched testimonials, an FAQ, and market-trusted credibility, then the page covers every must-have a direct-response sale needs.

signal.check: A sales page is missing 1 or more of the 8 must-haves, or urgency and scarcity on the page are not real.

risk.note: A structural build; ships as a full page, tested against the prior version.

prerequisites: Research base and offer maths from the offer domain
steps: Write a headline scored on the 7 traits.
Add real urgency and real scarcity, both true and enforced.
Add a guarantee designed as risk reversal, matching the real policy.
Explain the unique mechanism of both the problem and the solution.
Embed testimonials each with a named job, and build an FAQ that handles real objections.
Add credibility the market trusts, placed near checkout.

test.method: A/B test the rebuilt sales page against the current one.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Let copy and proof carry the sale; use design only to remove friction, never to impress
hypothesis: If a page clears a clean, familiar trust bar quickly and then spends effort on copy, proof and offer rather than heavy design, then conversion rises because visitors judge trust in milliseconds but decide to buy from the words and evidence.
does_not_apply_when: A high-ticket or premium brand where a polished, expensive-feeling design itself signals the price point

signal.check: A page invests heavily in animation or custom design elements that slow load time with no clear lift in trust or clarity.

risk.note: For high-ticket or premium brands, a clean, expensive-feeling design may itself be part of the trust signal; weigh this before stripping design.

steps: Check the page clears a clean, familiar, fast trust bar.
Cut animation or heavy design elements that slow load time without adding clarity.
Redirect the saved effort into copy, proof and offer quality.
For a high-ticket or premium brand, weigh whether the design itself is part of the price signal before stripping it.

test.method: Compare load time and conversion before and after removing heavy design elements.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Build a low-friction order page with obvious fields, quantity breaks, and real order bumps
hypothesis: If a custom order page has obvious card fields, quantity breaks, and 1 or 2 low-price order bumps that deliver a real service, then fewer buyers abandon at checkout and AOV rises from bumps buyers actually want.
does_not_apply_when: A store using native platform checkout with no custom order page

signal.check: An order page buries the card field, offers an order bump that changes nothing, such as fake shipping insurance, or has a cluttered design.

risk.note: Leaving native checkout can lose accelerated wallets and speed; weigh this trade-off first.

prerequisites: Contribution per buyer for each candidate order bump
steps: Make the card and CVV fields obvious and easy to find immediately.
Add quantity breaks where relevant.
Add 1 or 2 order bumps as checkboxes, each delivering a real service.
Price each bump against that SKU's own contribution per buyer, not a fixed price band.
Keep the design plain and fast.

test.method: Split test the order page design first, since it is usually the highest-impact single test in this funnel.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Offer a post-purchase upsell at peak emotion, priced by contribution per buyer
hypothesis: If the post-purchase offer presents 1 product chosen as more of the same or the solution to a real next problem, priced by contribution per buyer rather than a fixed multiple, then AOV rises without manufacturing a problem the product does not actually create.
does_not_apply_when: A one-off durable good with no natural next problem

signal.check: A post-purchase offer sells an unrelated or manufactured next problem, or is priced at a fixed multiple with no contribution check.

risk.note: A manufactured next problem is rejected outright; the next problem must be real.

prerequisites: Contribution per buyer for the candidate OTO product and price
steps: Choose 1 OTO product: more of the same, or the real next problem the first product creates.
Confirm the next problem is genuinely real, not manufactured.
Price the OTO by contribution per buyer, not a fixed multiple of the front-end price.
Route a yes to a second OTO and a no to a down-sell.

test.method: Split test the OTO product and price with the testing domain.
test.read_point: After the page's traffic floor is reached

title: Use a soft first ask for cold traffic; on a store, that means the cart drawer and express checkout
hypothesis: If cold traffic meets a low-friction first ask, an add-to-cart and express checkout on a store, rather than a high-friction ask up front, then more cold visitors take the first step instead of bouncing at a hard commitment.

signal.check: Cold traffic on a store is pushed toward a full account creation or a long form before any lower-friction first step, such as add to cart, is offered.

risk.note: For a store, the equivalent of a soft first ask is the cart drawer and express checkout, not a lead form.

steps: Confirm cold traffic is not asked for account creation or a long form before any purchase step.
Use add to cart into a cart drawer as the low-friction first step.
Offer express checkout options at the payment step.
Reserve any longer form for post-purchase or loyalty program signup, not the first ask.

test.method: Compare add-to-cart and checkout-start rate before and after simplifying the first ask.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Pull that SKU's own data, not a site average, before deciding what to fix
hypothesis: If a page's own GA4 and heatmap numbers are read instead of a site-wide average, then a single slow SKU is found and fixed instead of hiding behind a healthy brand-level conversion rate.

signal.check: A decision about a specific page was made from a site-wide average conversion rate instead of that page's own numbers.

risk.note: A data-reading discipline.

prerequisites: Page-level GA4 and heatmap access
steps: Pull GA4 and heatmap numbers for the specific page, not the site average.
Back every proposed change with 2 to 4 data points from that page.
Below about 25,000 to 30,000 monthly visitors on the page, or 50,000 to 80,000 for the whole store, add qualitative research: user tests, surveys, and review mining.
Use quantitative data to find where the problem is, and qualitative research to find why.

test.method: Track whether fixes based on page-level data outperform past fixes based on site averages.
test.read_point: After the next few page rebuilds

title: Fix the weakest GA4 funnel stage first, not the whole funnel at once
hypothesis: If the single weakest stage in the view-product to add-to-cart to checkout to purchase funnel is fixed first, then effort goes to the highest-leverage problem instead of being spread thin across every stage at once.

signal.check: A store or page audit tries to fix every funnel stage simultaneously with no ranking of which stage is weakest.

risk.note: Check GA4 event mapping before trusting any rate; a bad event setup can look like a bad funnel stage.

prerequisites: GA4 funnel rates for view product, add to cart, begin checkout, and purchase
steps: Check GA4 event mapping is correct before trusting any funnel rate.
Compute view-product, add-to-cart, begin-checkout, and purchase rates.
Identify the single weakest stage relative to what similar pages achieve.
Fix that stage first before moving to the next weakest.

test.method: Re-measure the funnel after fixing the weakest stage before touching any other stage.
test.read_point: After the fix has run a full business cycle

title: Read scroll maps mobile first at the average fold, 75, 50 and 25 percent lines
hypothesis: If scroll maps are read on mobile first at the average fold and the 75, 50 and 25 percent reach lines, then a key section reached by too few visitors, or a steep drop right after the fold, gets caught and moved up before it costs more sales.

signal.check: A key section is reached by about 30 percent or fewer visitors, or reach drops by about 50 percent right after the fold, with no plan to move that section up.

risk.note: A research step feeding a later layout change.

prerequisites: Scroll map tool installed and collecting on the page
steps: Open the scroll map for the page, starting with mobile.
Note the average fold and the 75, 50 and 25 percent reach lines.
Flag any key section reached by about 30 percent or fewer visitors to move up.
Flag a 50 percent drop right after the fold as a fold-leak problem.
Repeat on desktop after mobile.

test.method: Re-check the scroll map after moving a flagged section.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 weeks of traffic

title: Read click and area maps as clicks versus intent, not just raw click count
hypothesis: If click and area maps are read by comparing what is clicked now against what the brand wants clicked, then a CTA getting fewer clicks than a nearby testimonial link is caught as a red flag instead of being missed in the raw numbers.

signal.check: A CTA receives fewer clicks than a nearby non-CTA element, such as a testimonial link, with no flag raised.

risk.note: A research step feeding a later layout change.

prerequisites: Area map tool installed and collecting on the page
steps: Draw an area per element: image, price, reviews, each CTA, each nav item, filters, swatches.
Record click share per element.
Flag a CTA with fewer clicks than a nearby non-CTA element as a red flag.
Flag a clicked-but-not-clickable element as a false affordance, and a heavily clicked but small or low element to promote.
Cross-check high-click sections against scroll reach to find high-click, low-reach sections.

test.method: Re-check the area map after acting on a flagged finding.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 weeks of traffic

title: Watch converted-session recordings first, then rage clicks, to find repeated friction patterns
hypothesis: If session recordings are filtered to converted sessions first, then to rage clicks, and watched for patterns repeated across many sessions, then real friction points get found and fixed instead of guessed at from a single anecdote.

signal.check: No recordings have been reviewed for this page, or only a single recording was used to justify a change.

risk.note: A research step; watch at least 10 recordings before drawing a conclusion.

prerequisites: Session recording tool installed and collecting on the page
steps: Filter recordings to the order-confirmation path and watch 10 or more.
Log which sections converters read, where they pause, and what they click.
Filter separately to rage clicks and list the elements involved.
Look for a pattern repeated across several recordings before treating it as a real finding.
Re-check the same filter after a fix to confirm the pattern stops.

test.method: Re-run the same recording filter after a fix ships.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 weeks of traffic post-fix

title: Run 3 to 5 think-aloud user tests before any major redesign
hypothesis: If 3 to 5 think-aloud user tests are run with a first-impression question and real ecommerce tasks before a major page redesign, then the team learns why visitors struggle, not just where they drop off.

signal.check: A page redesign is planned with no think-aloud user test run, especially on a page below the traffic threshold for pure quantitative research.

risk.note: A modest cost per tester; budget it as a standard research line item.

prerequisites: A live page or clickable prototype
A user-testing tool with screening options
steps: Create a website test, 5 to 20 minutes, starting from scratch.
Ask a first-impression question before any scroll: what does this page sell and why should you care.
Give ecommerce tasks: find the right product, add to cart and check out, and share an overall impression.
Ask testers to walk through their thought process on every task.
Run 3 to 5 tests, log every hesitation and doubt, and re-run the same tasks after changes.

test.method: Re-run the same tasks with new testers after the redesign ships.
test.read_point: After the redesign, using the same task script

title: Mine reviews and surveys into ranked topics, motivations and anxieties before writing any new page
hypothesis: If reviews and survey answers are mined into topics, motivations, values and anxieties, tagged and pivoted by sentiment, then new page copy and proof choices come from ranked real data instead of a guess at what matters most.

signal.check: A new page is being written with no review or survey mining pass behind it.

risk.note: A research task; the output feeds the page brief and objection list.

prerequisites: Review exports from every platform the brand sells on
A post-purchase and mid-session survey, where available
steps: Export reviews from the site, Google, Trustpilot, and any marketplace into 1 sheet.
Tag each review's main topic, motivation, value, and anxiety.
Pivot positive and negative counts separately, computed in code.
Add sales-call and support-ticket objections to the same list.
Rank the top 5 objections and the top pains and desires, each with 3 verbatim quotes.

test.method: Track whether pages built from this mining pass need fewer revision rounds than pages built without it.
test.read_point: After the next few page builds

title: Compare device, entry path and landing-page anomalies before touching layout
hypothesis: If device, entry-path and landing-page performance are compared for anomalies, such as a large device gap or a path loop, before any layout change, then the real problem gets found instead of a guess at what to redesign.

signal.check: A page's mobile and desktop conversion or RPV differ sharply, or path exploration shows a repeated loop such as home to collection to home, with no investigation yet.

risk.note: A research step feeding a later fix.

prerequisites: GA4 path exploration and device-level reporting
steps: Compare conversion and RPV by device for this page.
Compare conversion for the same product from different entry URLs, such as homepage versus collection.
Compare engagement time on a top page against what is expected for the format.
Look for path loops, such as home to collection to home, which signal a findability problem.

test.method: Investigate any anomaly found and re-measure after the fix.
test.read_point: After the fix has run a full business cycle

title: Read the market's awareness stage from years of search trend data, cross-checked with revenue
hypothesis: If the market's stage, clueless, curious, or saturated, is read from years of category search trends and cross-checked against the brand's own revenue, then the headline and page framing match how much the market already knows instead of guessing the stage.

signal.check: A page's framing assumes a market stage, such as a contrarian claim for a curious market, with no search trend data checked to confirm it.

risk.note: Search interest measures attention, not sales; always cross-check with revenue.

prerequisites: Multi-year search trend data for the category term
steps: Pull multi-year search trend data for the category and brand terms.
Classify the market stage: clueless, curious, or saturated.
Cross-check the trend read against the brand's own revenue trend.
Match the page's framing, such as a contrarian headline for a curious market, to the confirmed stage.

test.method: Compare conversion on pages using the confirmed stage framing against pages using a guessed stage.
test.read_point: After the next full test cycle

title: Hand every test proposal to the testing team as a full if-then-because hypothesis
hypothesis: If every test proposal states the hypothesis as if we change X, then KPI moves, because of this data, along with the primary metric and the sources' prior with its weaknesses, then the testing team can size and run it without a back-and-forth.

signal.check: A test is proposed with no clear if-then-because hypothesis, no named primary metric, or no data points behind it.

risk.note: A proposal-format discipline, not a page change.

prerequisites: 2 to 4 data points supporting the hypothesis
steps: Write the hypothesis as if we change X, then KPI will move, because of this rationale.
Name the primary metric: purchase conversion, RPV, or contribution per visitor.
State the sources' prior for this idea and what it lacks.
Hand the proposal to the testing team with the page's weekly sessions and orders.

test.method: Track how many proposals need rework before the testing team can size them.
test.read_point: Ongoing, reviewed each test cycle

title: Use before-and-after reads under the traffic floor, and true A/B tests above it
hypothesis: If a page under its traffic floor uses a before-and-after read with a dated rollback point, and a page above the floor runs a true A/B test, then the store never mistakes an underpowered test for a real result.

signal.check: A low-traffic page is running a formal A/B test with no realistic chance of reaching significance, or a high-traffic page is only doing before-and-after reads.

risk.note: None of the sources give a true sample-size calculation; hand the real threshold to the testing domain.

prerequisites: Weekly sessions and orders for the page
steps: Check weekly sessions and orders for the page.
For a page clearly below a reasonable weekly-test threshold, use a before-and-after read with a dated rollback point.
For a page with enough traffic, run a true A/B test and let the testing domain set sample size and run length.
Never treat a source's rule-of-thumb traffic number as a real sample-size calculation.

test.method: Track outcomes by test type to see whether before-and-after reads on low-traffic pages hold up over time.
test.read_point: After several test cycles

title: Test above-the-fold elements first, 1 at a time, in a fixed order
hypothesis: If tests run above-the-fold elements first, headline, then hero image, then proof and FUD placement, 1 element at a time where traffic allows, then the highest-visibility changes get tested before smaller ones, and results stay attributable to a single change.

signal.check: Multiple unrelated elements are being changed in the same test, or a below-the-fold element is being tested before the hero has been tested.

risk.note: Bundle changes into 1 bigger test only where traffic does not support single-element tests.

steps: Test the headline first.
Test the hero image next.
Test proof and FUD placement third.
Change 1 element at a time where traffic allows; bundle changes only where it does not.
Set the primary metric and decision date before launch, and freeze other page changes during the test.

test.method: Track test sequence against this priority order.
test.read_point: Ongoing, reviewed each test cycle

title: Count conversions on a confirmation event; judge tests on purchases, never click-through alone
hypothesis: If tests are judged on a deduplicated purchase or confirmation event, with quiz and signup completions kept separate from purchases, then a test cannot look like a win on click-through or completion while actually losing money.

signal.check: A test is judged on click-through rate or quiz completion alone, with no purchase or RPV data included.

risk.note: A measurement discipline.

prerequisites: A deduplicated confirmation or success event
steps: Confirm conversions are counted on a confirmation page or a deduplicated success event.
Keep quiz and signup completions separate from purchase events.
Judge every test on purchases, RPV, and contribution, never click-through or completion alone.
Fix any tracking gap found during this check before trusting the test's result.

test.method: Audit test results against this measurement standard before accepting a winner.
test.read_point: Before declaring any test result final

title: Treat every lift figure in the source material as an example, never as a prior to expect
hypothesis: If a cited lift figure is treated as an unverified example with no sample size, duration, or isolation, rather than a number the store should expect, then decisions rest on the store's own future test results instead of another brand's marketing claim.

signal.check: A proposal cites a source's lift number, such as plus 64 percent, as if it were a reliable estimate for this store's own test.

risk.note: A documentation and evidence-labeling discipline.

steps: Read every cited lift figure for what it lacks: sample size, duration, isolation from other changes, significance, and whether the source sold the work that produced it.
Label the figure as an example, not a prior, in the proposal.
Never sum or average lift figures from different agency case studies to build a combined estimate.
Replace the label with the brand's own measured result once the test has run.

test.method: Check every new proposal for a properly labeled example versus prior before it is approved.
test.read_point: Before every test proposal is approved

title: Keep a steady test cadence and feed every result into ads and positioning
hypothesis: If tests run at a steady cadence set by the page's own traffic, and every result, win or loss, feeds back into ad angles and page positioning, then CRO work compounds into acquisition instead of staying siloed on 1 page.

signal.check: Test results are recorded but never shared with the team writing ad angles or other page copy.

risk.note: A process and reporting habit.

prerequisites: A shared log of test results, win or loss
steps: Record every test result, win or loss, with the reason.
Set test cadence by the page's own traffic, not a fixed 1-test-a-week rule for every page.
Share winning language and findings with the ad creative and copy teams.
Double down on a win with a follow-up test on the same idea before switching topics.

test.method: Track how many test findings get reused in ad copy or other pages within 1 quarter.
test.read_point: Quarterly

title: Finalize offer and copy before design starts; build the design around the words
hypothesis: If the offer and copy are finalized before design work begins, and design is built around that copy, then fewer pages need a rebuild after design locks in a layout the final copy does not fit.

signal.check: A design or template is being built before the offer and copy are finalized.

risk.note: A process-sequencing rule.

prerequisites: A completed wireframe with copy
steps: Finalize the offer, price and copy before any design work starts.
Hand the design team a wireframe with copy, not a blank template to fill.
Build the visual design around the final copy's length and structure.
Avoid trimming finished copy to fit a design decided in advance.
