test.method: Track rework hours on pages built copy-first against pages built design-first.
test.read_point: After the next several page builds

title: Run the full pre-traffic QA checklist before sending any traffic to a new page
hypothesis: If every new page passes message match, claims audit, disclosure, policy match, tracking, mobile, and speed checks before traffic starts, then the store avoids the most common launch mistakes: broken tracking, mismatched offers, and compliance gaps.

signal.check: A page is about to go live with no completed pre-traffic QA checklist.

risk.note: A checklist gate before launch; keep the previous page version and destination as a rollback.

prerequisites: Tracking installed and testable on the page
steps: Check message match between the live ad and the page.
Run the claims audit and confirm the disclosure label where required.
Confirm policy, price and offer match on every step from ad to checkout.
Submit a test order or form in each variant and confirm the confirmation event fires once.
Check every device width, tap targets, and the pinned CTA.
Run a speed test and confirm it meets the target.
Proofread for typos, placeholder text, and invented numbers.
Confirm no API keys are in page JavaScript, then set a rollback point before launch.

test.method: Run this checklist before every launch, with every row passing.
test.read_point: Before every launch

title: Read the first 48 hours after launch and fix the step where the funnel loses people
hypothesis: If the first 48 hours after a launch are read for page-to-page click-through and cost anomalies, and the losing step is fixed quickly, then a bad launch gets caught and corrected before it wastes a full week of spend.

signal.check: A page launched more than 48 hours ago with no review of click-through, CTR, or CPM anomalies yet.

risk.note: A monitoring habit right after launch.

prerequisites: A written plan naming who reads which metrics in the first 48 hours
steps: Write a first-48-hours plan naming the metrics to read and who reads them.
Check page-to-page click-through and CTR or CPM anomalies after launch.
Identify the step in the funnel losing the most people.
Fix that step quickly rather than waiting for a full test cycle to end.

test.method: Compare spend efficiency in the first week for pages with and without a 48-hour review.
test.read_point: 1 week after launch

title: Treat a landing page as a living asset that keeps improving, not a one-and-done build
hypothesis: If a page keeps receiving new proof, tests, and refinements after launch instead of being treated as finished, then it keeps improving for years instead of decaying as the market and creative around it change.

signal.check: A page has not been revisited, tested, or updated with new proof since its original launch.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source reports winners running 5 to 7 years across 40 to 60 pages tested to find one, its own experience

risk.note: A cadence and mindset, not a 1-time task.

prerequisites: A backlog of test and improvement ideas for the page
steps: Schedule a recurring review of the page's performance and proof freshness.
Add new proof as it becomes available, such as new reviews or a new press mention.
Keep testing 1 element at a time rather than declaring the page finished.
Track whether a page's performance has decayed since its last update.

test.method: Compare conversion trend for pages under continuous improvement against pages left untouched.
test.read_point: Quarterly

title: Write a 1-page brief before building any page: audience, pain, outcome, awareness, type, event
hypothesis: If a 1-page brief fixes the audience, pain, outcome, awareness stage, page type, and the 1 conversion event before any copy is written, then the build starts from a clear decision instead of drifting mid-draft.

signal.check: A page build starts with no written brief covering persona, pain, awareness stage, page type, and conversion event.

risk.note: The brief is a document; it does not touch a live page.

prerequisites: Brand record and traffic data available
steps: Name the 1 persona this page is for, backed by real buyer data, not a guess.
Name the pain or desire bringing them, with at least 3 verbatim quotes attached.
Name the functional and emotional outcome they want.
Name the traffic's awareness stage, the page type, and the 1 conversion event.
Paste in the ad's exact promise, hook, persona and offer, if paid traffic feeds the page.
Note constraints: claims list, banned claims, policy terms, price, stock, and brand voice.
Do not proceed to drafting if the ad's promise or the proven-angle status cannot be filled in.

test.method: Track how many revision rounds a page needs with a completed brief versus without one.
test.read_point: After the next several page builds

title: Use AI to draft the first advertorial version from the research base, then scrub every invented fact
hypothesis: If an AI tool drafts the first advertorial version strictly from the written research base and a swipe used for structure only, then scrubs the output for any invented person, study, number, or price, the team gets a fast first draft with no hallucinated fact reaching the page.

signal.check: An AI-assisted advertorial draft is being used with no verification pass for invented people, studies, numbers, or prices.

risk.note: The draft is a starting point; nothing ships until every fact is matched to the brand record.

prerequisites: Completed research base as clean text or PDFs
A swipe chosen for structure only
Current disclosure wording
steps: Prime the AI tool with the brand's own product facts and the research base; confirm it understands before drafting.
Run an extraction pass for market, pains, promises, proof, common solutions and why they fail, and product facts.
Attach the swipe and ask only for structure analysis, then draft using the brand's own facts and fixed variables.
Draft in sections, reading and correcting as it goes rather than accepting a full draft blind.
Ask for alternative headlines and run tightening prompts for flow, simple language, and standalone subheads.
Scrub the draft: remove any invented expert, study, testimonial, or price; set the real CTA link and disclosure label.

test.method: Track the number of invented facts caught per draft over time.
test.read_point: After each new advertorial draft

title: Run a structured tighten pass on every advertorial draft before it goes to design
hypothesis: If every advertorial draft goes through a structured tighten pass, naming the frame, color-coding pain and mechanism, auditing the story-stop point, and reading subheads alone, then weak spots get caught before the page is built, not after it launches.

signal.check: An advertorial moves to design with no structured review pass beyond a single read-through.

risk.note: A review checklist; catches issues cheaply before design work is spent.

prerequisites: A completed advertorial draft
steps: Name the frame in 1 word and confirm it holds to the end.
Color-code pain, desire and mechanism to confirm every section mixes all 3.
Search for the mechanism name to confirm only 1 name is used throughout.
Run the story-stop audit and read only the subheads in order.
Move proof up if none appears in the lead, and add CTAs earlier if the first sits too low.
Run a reading-level check and a claims-and-people check before handing off to design.

test.method: Track how many issues the tighten pass catches per draft over time.
test.read_point: After each new advertorial draft

title: Write a full quiz spec covering questions, branching, tracking and results before handing it to a builder
hypothesis: If a full quiz spec lists every question's text, input type, job label, and branch logic, plus the results-page order, tracking events, and reporting cadence, then the builder implements it correctly the first time and the analyst can measure it from day one.

signal.check: A quiz is being built from a rough outline instead of a full spec covering questions, branching, tracking and reporting.

risk.note: A documentation task before the build starts.

prerequisites: Research base and the rule mapping answers to SKUs
steps: List every question with its text, input type, options, job label, and whether it changes the recommendation.
Write the info screens with their copy and the data behind any number shown.
Write the capture step's consent wording and gate decision.
Write the results-page block order and copy.
List every tracking event: start, step views, completion, capture, and purchase after quiz.
Set the export and reporting cadence, and the first-3-question test plan.
Test the spec with 3 contradictory answer sets before handing it to the builder.

test.method: Track builder rework requests for quizzes built from a full spec versus a rough outline.
test.read_point: After the next few quiz builds

title: Score every candidate test with a fixed checklist and hand over a ranked backlog
hypothesis: If every candidate test is scored on a fixed checklist, such as above the fold, noticeable in 5 seconds, raises motivation, and high-traffic page, and the whole ranked backlog is handed over at once, then the testing team can queue the next test without waiting on a fresh write-up each time.

signal.check: Tests are proposed 1 at a time with no shared scoring sheet or backlog, so the testing team has nothing queued once the current test ends.

risk.note: A backlog-management habit.

prerequisites: A list of candidate tests with their data points
steps: List every candidate test with its page, hypothesis, and data points.

Score each on a fixed checklist: above the fold, noticeable in 5 seconds, adds or removes an element, raises motivation, high-traffic page, addresses a user-test finding, supported by heatmaps, ease of build.
Rank the backlog by score, highest first.
Hand over the full ranked backlog, not just the top candidate, so the next test is always ready to queue.

test.method: Track how often the testing team has a queued test ready versus waiting on a new write-up.
test.read_point: Ongoing, reviewed each test cycle

title: Reveal extra form fields only after the first one is filled
hypothesis: If a lead, quiz-email or contact form shows 1 simple field first and reveals the rest only after the shopper fills it, then completion rises because the form never looks long at the first glance.

signal.check: A form on a lead page, quiz email gate or contact page shows every field at once and completion is below the store's own baseline.

risk.note: Reveals fields in steps; nothing is removed, so a rollback is a simple toggle.

prerequisites: A form builder or theme that supports conditional or staged field reveal
steps: List every field the form asks for and pick the 1 simplest one to show first, usually email.
Hide the rest of the fields until the first one is filled.
Reveal the remaining fields in the same view once the first field has a valid entry.
Keep field labels visible, not only placeholder text, once revealed.
A/B test the staged form against the all-at-once version on the same traffic.

test.method: Split test the staged form against showing all fields at once.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Move a proof section higher when scroll data shows few visitors reach it
hypothesis: If a proof or value section is reached by only a small share of visitors on the scroll map, then moving it higher and tightening everything above it raises how many people see it before they decide.

signal.check: A scroll map shows a key proof, case-study or value section reached by well under half of visitors while an earlier section is mostly empty space.

risk.note: Reordering sections is a layout change with an easy rollback.

prerequisites: A scroll-depth heatmap or analytics report for the page
steps: Read the scroll map and note the reach percentage at each section boundary.
Flag any section the brand considers important that is reached by well under half of visitors.
Cut or tighten the sections above it that are not earning their space.
Move the under-reached section higher, or shorten the page so it arrives sooner.
Re-check the scroll map after the change.

test.method: Compare the section's reach percentage before and after the reorder.
test.read_point: After enough sessions accumulate on the new layout

title: Contact a high-intent lead within 1 minute of their action
hypothesis: If a high-ticket or consult-style store calls or texts a shopper within about 1 minute of a quiz completion or contact-form submit, then more of them convert because the interest has not yet cooled.
does_not_apply_when: A low-ticket, self-serve product where nobody expects or wants a phone call

signal.check: A high-ticket or made-to-order product collects quiz completions or consult requests but the team's first outreach happens hours or days later.

risk.note: Automating outreach can misfire if the trigger event is wrong; test with dummy submissions first.

prerequisites: A phone, SMS or chat tool that can trigger from a form or quiz submit event
A team or on-call rep who can respond within minutes
steps: Pick the 1 high-intent action that should trigger immediate contact, such as a quiz completion or consult request.
Wire that event to an automatic call, text or chat alert to a rep.
Set a target of contacting the lead within about 1 minute.
Test the trigger with dummy submissions before going live.
Track lead-to-customer rate for fast-contacted leads against the old response time.

test.method: Compare lead-to-customer conversion for leads contacted within 1 minute against the store's prior average response time.
test.read_point: After enough leads pass through both response times to compare

title: Ramp newly generated keyword pages slowly instead of publishing hundreds at once
hypothesis: If a store publishes new keyword or location-matched landing pages a handful at a time instead of hundreds in a single day, then it avoids a search-engine penalty that a sudden mass of near-duplicate pages can trigger.

signal.check: A store is about to publish, or has just published, a large batch of automatically generated city, keyword or angle pages in a single day.

risk.note: A search penalty from mass publishing can take time to reverse, so this is safer to prevent than to fix.

prerequisites: A page-generation skill or template that can output more pages than should be published at once
steps: Set a daily or weekly cap on how many new keyword pages go live.
Publish in that capped batch, not all at once.
Watch organic indexing and rankings for the new pages after each batch.
Slow the rate further if indexed pages drop or a manual action notice appears.

test.method: Track indexed page count and organic ranking for the new pages after each publish batch.
test.read_point: After each publish batch, checked weekly

title: Make each test's winner the new control for the next challenger
hypothesis: If every A/B test's winning variant becomes the new control for the next challenger instead of testing new ideas against the original page each time, then gains compound instead of resetting with every test.

signal.check: The store keeps testing new variants against the same original page instead of against the last confirmed winner.

risk.note: Requires discipline to update the control page after every win; no downside if followed.

prerequisites: A test log that records which variant is the current control
steps: After a test declares a winner, make that variant the new control page.
Design the next challenger to beat the new control, not the original page.
Log the control change and the date it took effect.
Repeat every cycle so the page keeps improving from its best known state.

test.method: Track cumulative conversion lift across a sequence of tests where the control rolls forward.
test.read_point: After several test cycles

title: Bridge the mechanism through a familiar intermediary to reach new pain points
hypothesis: If an advertorial names a familiar intermediary concept the product works through, such as detox or circulation, then the brand can ask what other real pains relate to that intermediary and open new, tested angles beyond the current one.

signal.check: A brand has only tested 1 or 2 angles for a product whose mechanism plausibly relates to several real pain points.

risk.note: New angles must still be truthful and cannot claim disease or medical outcomes without support.

prerequisites: The product's real, verifiable mechanism
A list of the product's proven pain-point angles so far
steps: Name the familiar concept the product's mechanism works through, such as detox, circulation or lymph flow.
List other real, common problems that relate to that same concept.
Rank the new candidate pains by urgency, scale and relevance.
Write the causal bridge from the new pain back to the mechanism for each candidate.
Test the strongest new angle as a small campaign before committing spend.

test.method: A/B test the new angle's ad and page against the current best-performing angle on a capped budget.
test.read_point: After the new angle reaches a meaningful spend level

title: Reject a big idea unless product, market and prospect all overlap
hypothesis: If a candidate advertorial big idea is tested against product uniqueness, current market state and the chosen prospect segment, and only kept when it fits all three, then the brand avoids shipping a generic or ungrounded angle.

signal.check: A candidate big idea for an advertorial or campaign fits only 1 or 2 of product uniqueness, market state and prospect segment.

risk.note: A rejected idea costs only the time already spent drafting it.

prerequisites: A written list of the product's unique parts
A read on the market's current beliefs and competing products
A named prospect segment
steps: Write what is unique about the product, its combination of parts, or its origin story.
Write the market's current live debate and where the majority's beliefs sit.
Write which prospect segment the idea is meant to reach.
Score each candidate big idea against all 3: does it use the unique product fact, fit the market state, and speak to this segment.
Drop any idea that scores on only 1 or 2 of the 3.

test.method: Compare hook rate for ideas that passed the 3-way check against ideas that did not.
test.read_point: After each tested idea reaches a meaningful spend level

title: Write a truthful reason for every product component before drafting proof
hypothesis: If every part of the product, its form, ingredient or source, gets a written and truthful reason it is exactly that way, then the page can answer 'why this instead of the alternative' honestly instead of leaning on vague quality claims.

signal.check: A page claims a product is better or different with no stated reason tied to a specific component.

risk.note: This only requires research and writing; no product change.

prerequisites: Real, verifiable facts about the product's components, sourcing and manufacturing
steps: List every component of the product: form, ingredient or material, source, dose or amount.
For each, write the strongest truthful reason it is that way rather than the common alternative.
Do not invent a feature or an advantage the component does not have.
Use the strongest of these reasons in the proof or mechanism section of the page.

test.method: A/B test the page with component-level justifications against the current version.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Only tie a trend hook to a trend the target market already knows about
hypothesis: If a trend-based hook is checked against real, current public awareness of that trend before it ships, instead of the marketer's own early exposure to it, then the hook lands as familiar concern rather than confusing or overreaching claims.

signal.check: A page or ad leans on a trend, such as a health scare or ingredient concern, that the marketer knows about but has not confirmed the target market has heard of.

risk.note: Skipping a trend hook that is not yet known costs only that 1 angle.

prerequisites: A way to check public search or social interest in the trend
steps: Search the trend term to see how much public search or social interest already exists.
Check whether the target market's own conversations or reviews already mention the trend.
Ship the trend hook only if the market already shows real awareness.
If awareness is thin, use a slower education approach instead of assuming the reader already worries about it.

test.method: Compare hook rate for trend-based hooks that passed the awareness check against ones that did not.
test.read_point: After each trend-based ad reaches a meaningful spend level

title: Build a why-now layer stating what changed to make the problem newly relevant
hypothesis: If a page states what has genuinely risen or fallen in the world that makes the customer's problem newly relevant today, then the reader's guard lowers because the cause is framed as external, not a personal failing.

signal.check: A page states a problem and a solution but never explains why the problem exists more now than before.

risk.note: Every 'something rose, something fell' claim must be a real, sourced fact, not an invented trend.

prerequisites: A real, verifiable fact about what has changed in the category or environment
steps: Research what has genuinely risen (a new exposure, habit or condition) that relates to the problem.
Research what has genuinely fallen (a protective habit or resource) that used to offset it.
Write 1 short section stating both, framed as an external cause, not the reader's fault.
Verify every fact used before publishing.

test.method: A/B test the page with a why-now section against the version without it.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Build an expert-confession body only with a real, consenting expert
hypothesis: If the advertorial body is built as a credentialed expert's account of a pivotal patient question, an upstream root-cause answer, an analogy and a timeline contrast, then it earns hope and credibility, but only when a real, verifiable expert has agreed to be named.
does_not_apply_when: No real, willing, qualified expert exists for the brand

signal.check: A brand has, or can recruit, a real qualified expert willing to be named, and the current advertorial uses a generic or vague narrator instead.

risk.note: An invented or unverified expert is a compliance and trust risk; only proceed with a real, consenting person.

prerequisites: A real expert willing to be named and quoted
Written consent from that expert
steps: Confirm a real, qualified expert exists and has agreed to be featured and quoted.
Write the expert's credential in 1 line.
Write the pivotal question a real patient or customer asked that reframed the cause.
Give the upstream root-cause answer, an analogy that matches its real action, and a timeline contrast.
Follow with proof and the offer, and verify every fact and figure before publishing.

test.method: A/B test the expert-confession structure against the current advertorial structure.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Split ad and page tests across a fixed portfolio of awareness levels
hypothesis: If new ad and page tests are deliberately spread across a starting split of unaware, problem-aware and more-aware angles instead of only testing near the current best angle, then the brand can find a wider-reaching angle instead of only refining a narrow one.

signal.check: A brand's test backlog only refines variants of its current best-performing awareness level, with no tests at the other levels.

risk.note: Unaware-level tests fail more often; keep the spend on them capped while testing.

prerequisites: A classification of current ads and pages by awareness level
Enough test budget to run more than 1 angle at once
steps: Classify current ads and pages by awareness level: unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, most-aware.
Set a starting split of test budget across at least 2 of those levels, weighted toward the levels with least coverage.
Run each level's test to a decision point.
Rebalance future test budget toward whichever level's tests win, based on the brand's own results.

test.method: Compare cost per result across awareness levels tested under the portfolio split.
test.read_point: After each awareness-level test reaches a meaningful spend level

title: Build a visual demonstration when the product's benefit is invisible
hypothesis: If the product's benefit is hard to see or believe, then a hero demonstration, either a reader self-test, a staged proof event, or a prop that reveals the invisible mechanism, proves the claim faster than stating it in words.

signal.check: The hero media is a plain product shot even though the product's main benefit cannot be seen or believed from a photo alone.

risk.note: The demonstration must show the product's real action; exaggerate staging, never the result.

prerequisites: A real product mechanism that can be shown or tested visually
steps: Identify the 1 outcome that can be shown in a single glance.
Pick 1 type: a test the reader can do themselves, a staged proof event, or a prop that makes an invisible mechanism visible.
Film or shoot it with the real product, not a stand-in.
Use it as the hero image or video and check platform claim rules before publishing.

test.method: A/B test the demonstration hero against the current product-only hero.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Call out a distinct sensory cue for consumable products to protect repeat orders
hypothesis: If a consumable product has a distinct, real sensory or use cue that customers notice, and the brand calls it out in PDP and post-purchase copy, then customers learn to judge 'it's working' by that cue, which protects repeat orders against copycats that lack it.

signal.check: A consumable product has a real, distinct sensory or use cue (taste, texture, sensation, timing) that is not currently mentioned in PDP or post-purchase copy.

risk.note: Only claim a cue the product genuinely has; do not invent a sensation.

prerequisites: A real, distinct, repeatable sensory or use cue in the product
steps: Identify a real sensory or physical cue customers notice when using the product correctly.
Add a line in the PDP and unboxing or first-use copy naming that cue and what it means.
Repeat the cue callout in a post-purchase or replenishment email.
Track repeat purchase rate for customers who saw the cue callout against those who did not.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase rate for cohorts that received the sensory-cue messaging against those that did not.
test.read_point: After 1 full replenishment cycle

title: Blame the tool or method, not the buyer, when framing the problem
hypothesis: If advertorial or PDP copy frames the customer's ongoing problem as caused by the tool or method they currently use, not by their own effort or care, then the reader stays receptive instead of feeling accused.

signal.check: A page's problem section implies the reader is lazy, careless or at fault, rather than pointing at the tool or method they use.

risk.note: Reframe must stay honest; do not blame a specific real competitor without proof.

prerequisites: A real reason the common tool or method falls short
steps: Identify the tool or method the customer currently uses that genuinely underperforms.
Rewrite the problem section to name that tool or method as the cause, not the reader's habits.
Follow with the mechanism that explains why the tool falls short and what the product does differently.
Read the section back as the customer would, checking it does not read as an accusation.

test.method: A/B test the tool-blame framing against a version that implies the reader's fault.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Anchor price against the real cost of the problem, not a competitor price
hypothesis: If a real, sourced figure exists for what it costs to leave the problem unsolved, then anchoring the product's price against that cost, instead of only a competitor's price, makes the price feel small next to the consequence.

signal.check: A real, checkable cost of the unsolved problem exists (a repair cost, a replacement cost, a lost-time cost) but the page only compares price to competitors or a discount.

risk.note: Only use a real, sourced cost figure; never invent or round up a consequence cost.

prerequisites: A real, sourced figure for the cost of the unsolved problem
steps: Research and source a real figure for what the unsolved problem typically costs the customer.
State that figure plainly next to the product's price.
Frame the product price as small against that cost, not just against a competitor's price.
Cite or footnote where the cost figure comes from if it could be questioned.

test.method: A/B test the cost-of-problem price anchor against the current price presentation.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Close an advertorial with a genuine comment or Q&A section
hypothesis: If an advertorial or presell page ends with real customer comments and questions, or a clearly labeled FAQ where no real comments exist yet, then last-minute questions get answered in the reader's own words instead of leaving the page on a pitch.

signal.check: An advertorial or presell page ends right after the CTA with no space for real reader questions or reactions.

risk.note: Never fabricate a comment thread; use only real comments or a clearly labeled FAQ.

prerequisites: Real customer comments, questions or a genuine FAQ list
steps: Collect real customer questions and reactions from support, reviews or an actual comment feed.
Build a closing section showing those real comments, or a clearly labeled FAQ if none exist yet.
Include a short shipping, stock or product question and its honest answer.
Never write a fake comment thread or persona.

test.method: A/B test the page with a genuine closing comment or FAQ section against the version without one.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Add a quick add-to-cart control on collection tiles
hypothesis: If path data shows many add-to-carts require a detour through the PDP after a collection page, then adding a quick add-to-cart control on the collection tile removes that detour and lets ready buyers convert faster.

signal.check: Path analysis shows a large share of add-to-carts happen only after collection to PDP to add-to-cart, rather than directly from the collection page.

risk.note: A quick-add control must not skip a required choice such as size or shade; route those to the PDP instead.

prerequisites: Path or funnel data showing collection to PDP to add-to-cart flow
A theme or app that supports a quick add-to-cart tile
steps: Pull a path report from the collection page to add-to-cart, noting how many go through the PDP.
For SKUs with no required size or variant choice, add a quick add-to-cart button on the collection tile.
For SKUs with a required choice, keep the tile linking to the PDP.
A/B test the collection page with quick add against the current version.

test.method: A/B test the collection page with quick add-to-cart against the current version.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Trigger a mid-session survey asking what's holding the visitor back
hypothesis: If a short on-page survey fires at about 60% of the page's average session duration and asks whether anything is holding the visitor back from buying, then the store collects live objection data instead of waiting for a post-purchase or exit survey.

signal.check: The brand has no way to learn why an active but not-yet-buying visitor is hesitating, only after-the-fact reviews or exit surveys.

risk.note: Watch that the survey pop-up itself does not suppress conversion for the sessions it interrupts.

prerequisites: A survey or on-site pop-up tool
The page's average session duration
steps: Find the page's average session duration from analytics.
Set the survey to trigger at about 60% of that duration.
Ask a simple yes or no: is anything holding you back from buying right now.
If yes, offer preset reasons plus a free-text option for anything else.
Route the themes into the test backlog and watch whether the survey itself affects conversion.

test.method: Compare conversion rate for sessions shown the survey against sessions not shown it.
test.read_point: After enough sessions accumulate to compare the 2 groups

title: Batch advertorial drafts by pairing avatars with proven structures
lever: batch draft production, test backlog speed
hypothesis: If each researched avatar archetype is paired with a different proven structural swipe, changing 1 variable at a time, then the team can produce a backlog of testable advertorial drafts fast instead of writing and reviewing 1 draft at a time.

signal.check: A brand has more than 1 researched avatar archetype but only 1 advertorial draft exists to test them all.

risk.note: Every draft still needs the same claims and proof check before it can run; batching speed does not skip that step.

prerequisites: A completed research base with more than 1 avatar archetype
More than 1 proven advertorial structure to model
steps: List the researched avatar archetypes for the product.
List the proven structures available to model, keeping structure only, not claims or text.
Pair each avatar with 1 structure, changing only 1 of the 2 per draft so results can be attributed.
Draft each pairing, then run the compliance and claims check on every draft before it goes live.
Queue the drafts into the test backlog.

test.method: Track how many reviewed, compliant drafts the team can produce per week with and without batching.
test.read_point: After 1 batching cycle

title: List the core beliefs a buyer must hold and check each is covered
hypothesis: If a store lists the 4 to 6 beliefs a buyer must hold to purchase, drawn from real customer research, and checks each has a supporting page element, then no belief gap is left for the reader to fill with doubt.

signal.check: A page has no documented list of the beliefs a buyer needs to hold before buying, so gaps are found only by guesswork.

risk.note: Every belief must come from real research, not assumption, or the page ends up arguing points buyers do not actually doubt.

prerequisites: Customer research: reviews, support tickets, survey answers or interviews
steps: From real customer research, write 4 to 6 'I believe that...' statements a buyer must hold to purchase.
Map each belief to the page element that supports it: a testimonial, the mechanism section, an FAQ answer or a credibility block.
Flag any belief with no supporting element and add one.
Re-check coverage whenever the page is edited.

test.method: A/B test the page with full belief coverage against the current version.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Pick the post-purchase upsell with a more-of-same or next-problem framework
hypothesis: If the post-purchase upsell offer is chosen from 1 of 2 frameworks, either more of the same product at a discount or a product that solves the new problem the front-end product just created, then the upsell has a clear logic instead of being an arbitrary add-on.

signal.check: A store's post-purchase upsell offer was picked without a stated reason tied to the front-end product's natural next need.

risk.note: Only offer a next-problem product that genuinely follows from using the first one; do not manufacture a problem.

prerequisites: The front-end product's typical usage pattern and any known follow-on need
steps: Check whether the front-end product is naturally bought again in larger quantity (more-of-same fits).
Or check whether using the front-end product creates or reveals a new, real problem (next-problem fits).
Pick the upsell product using whichever framework fits the front-end product.
Price and test the upsell against a control of no offer or the current generic upsell.

test.method: A/B test the framework-chosen upsell against the current post-purchase offer.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Trigger a help pop-up at the exact point visitors abandon reading
hypothesis: If a help-plus-discount pop-up fires at the exact scroll-depth point where heatmap data shows visitors abandon a page, instead of only a generic exit-intent trigger, then the offer reaches people at the moment they are actually losing interest.

signal.check: A scroll-depth heatmap shows a clear drop-off point mid-page, but the store's only pop-up trigger is exit intent or a fixed time delay.

risk.note: Stacking a scroll-depth discount on top of other pop-ups can condition shoppers to wait for a discount; watch margin impact.

prerequisites: A heatmap or scroll-depth tool
A pop-up tool that can trigger on scroll position
steps: Read the scroll-depth heatmap to find the point where a clear share of visitors stop scrolling or leave.
Set a pop-up to trigger at that scroll position, offering help or a modest discount.
A/B test against exit-intent-only or no pop-up.
Judge on sales and margin, not pop-up views.

test.method: A/B test the scroll-triggered pop-up against the current exit-intent-only setup.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Set equal step savings across bundle tiers to steer to the target tier
hypothesis: If bundle tier savings are structured so the step up to the middle tier and the step up to the top tier are the same dollar amount, matched to the tier most buyers actually need, then the middle tier reads as the obvious deal without a hard sell.

signal.check: Bundle tiers exist but the incremental saving from tier to tier is uneven or arbitrary, with no tier clearly built to feel like the best deal.

risk.note: The target tier must be the one that genuinely fits most buyers' real usage, not just the most profitable one.

prerequisites: Order data showing which tier most buyers actually need or use
steps: Find which tier size most buyers realistically need, from order history or usage data.
Set the saving from the smallest tier to that target tier and from the target tier to the top tier as the same dollar amount.
State each saving plainly in the tier headline.
A/B test the restructured tiers against the current pricing.

test.method: A/B test the restructured bundle tiers against the current tier pricing.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Route a comparison advertorial for retargeting into an on-site quiz
hypothesis: If a comparison-style advertorial honestly ranks real category options for retargeting traffic and routes the click into an on-site quiz for a personalized recommendation, then the visitor arrives at the product pre-sold and only checking fit before price shows.

signal.check: Retargeting traffic for a brand with more than 1 real SKU or use case lands directly on a single PDP with no comparison or personalization step.

risk.note: Ranking real competitors honestly avoids comparative-advertising risk; do not discredit alternatives without proof.

prerequisites: A real, honest comparison of category options
An existing or buildable on-site quiz
steps: Research the real alternatives shoppers actually weigh in the category.
Write an honest comparison ranking them, including the brand's own product without artificially placing it first.
Route the comparison page's CTA into an on-site quiz for a personalized fit recommendation.
Show the recommendation and price only after the quiz.
A/B test this route against sending retargeting traffic straight to the PDP.

test.method: A/B test the comparison-to-quiz route against direct-to-PDP retargeting on the same audience.
test.read_point: After the test reaches a meaningful spend level

title: Build a 2-page pre-sell funnel that reveals price only on page 2
hypothesis: If cold traffic sees a page 1 that reveals the product and mechanism and only reaches price on page 2, then the hidden-price variant can be judged on purchase rate after the click instead of assumed to help or hurt.

signal.check: A single long advertorial reveals price on the same page as the mechanism, with no test of a 2-page split.

risk.note: A hidden price can read as a bait step if the click-through to page 2 is not judged on purchases after the click.

prerequisites: An existing 1-page advertorial to split into 2 pages
steps: Split the current advertorial into 2 pages: page 1 covers the problem, story and mechanism; page 2 covers the offer, price and guarantee.
Put a clear CTA at the end of page 1 leading to page 2.
A/B test the 2-page version against the current 1-page version on the same cold traffic.
Judge on purchase rate after the click, not on the click-through to page 2 alone.

test.method: A/B test the 2-page funnel against the current 1-page advertorial, judged on purchase rate after the click.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Show reviews from repeat buyers as proof of continuity for consumables
hypothesis: If a consumable product's proof section includes reviews specifically from repeat buyers on their second order or later, then shoppers see continuity proof, not just a first impression, which matters most for products bought again and again.

signal.check: A consumable PDP shows only first-purchase reviews with no signal of which reviewers have reordered.

risk.note: Only tag a review as a repeat-buyer review if the order history actually confirms it.

prerequisites: A review platform or process that can flag a reviewer's order count
steps: Identify reviews from customers on their second order or later, using order history where the review platform allows it.
Add 1 or 2 of these reviews to the PDP's proof section, labeled as a repeat customer.
Keep first-purchase reviews too; do not replace them.
A/B test the page with repeat-buyer reviews included against the current review mix.

test.method: A/B test the page with repeat-buyer reviews against the current review selection.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Present a bundle as a value stack against its summed item value
hypothesis: If a bundle or kit lists each included item with its own real value, sums them, and shows the bundle price against that sum, then the discount feels concrete instead of relying on a bare feature list or a simple percent-off.

signal.check: A bundle or kit page lists its contents as a feature list or a simple percent-off with no itemized value shown for each part.

risk.note: Every itemized value must be a real, defensible price, not an inflated reference price.

prerequisites: A real, defensible individual price for every item in the bundle
steps: List every item included in the bundle or kit.
State each item's own real individual price.
Sum the individual prices and show the bundle price against that sum.
A/B test the value-stack presentation against the current bundle listing.

test.method: A/B test the value-stack bundle presentation against the current listing.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Diagnose which of 3 growth stages the page's funnel is in before fixing it
hypothesis: If a store first diagnoses whether traffic arrives but does not convert, converts about average with scale risk ahead, or already converts well and just needs more from the same traffic, then the team fixes offer and copy, prepares for a spend jump, or runs CRO, instead of guessing which lever to pull.

signal.check: A team is about to invest in a page rebuild or a CRO program without first checking which growth stage the store's funnel is actually in.

risk.note: This is a triage step, not a fix; it only points to which fix to run next.

prerequisites: Conversion rate and CPA history
A rough sense of current and planned ad spend
steps: Check whether traffic converts poorly regardless of source: if so, fix offer and copy first.
Check whether conversion is about average but a spend increase is planned: if so, stress-test the page before scaling spend.
Check whether spend is already high with decent conversion: if so, run CRO on the existing page instead of chasing more traffic.
Pick the matching fix and revisit this check after major spend changes.

test.method: Track conversion rate and CPA before and after the matched fix is applied.
test.read_point: After the matched fix has run for a full cycle

title: Reposition around a non-price desire when buyers are price-motivated
hypothesis: If customer research shows the main buying motive is finding the cheapest option, then repositioning the page around a non-price desire, such as a real mechanism, trust or uniqueness, keeps the brand out of a race to the bottom against mass retailers it cannot out-price.

signal.check: Customer research or reviews show price is the dominant stated motive, and the page's main selling argument is also price.

risk.note: This is a positioning shift, not a price change; it can take time to move buyer perception.

prerequisites: Customer research showing the buyer's real motive
A real, defensible non-price differentiator
steps: Confirm from real research that price is the dominant stated buying motive.
Identify a real, defensible non-price differentiator: mechanism, sourcing, trust, or a use case mass retailers do not serve.
Rewrite the page's main argument around that differentiator instead of price comparison.
Test the repositioned page against the current price-led page on the same traffic.

test.method: A/B test the repositioned page against the current price-led page.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Show the shopper's own quiz answers as a personalized progress visual
hypothesis: If a quiz shows the shopper's own inputs back as a personalized progress visual mid-quiz, such as a timeline from today to a stated goal, computed only from real data, then the shopper feels the quiz is building something real for them without any invented projection.

signal.check: A quiz collects numeric or goal-related answers but never reflects them back to the shopper before the results page.

risk.note: Never simulate a computation or invent a projected outcome; only show what the entered data honestly supports.

prerequisites: Quiz inputs that support a real, honest computed visual (a date range, a size comparison)
steps: Identify which quiz answers can support a real, honestly computed visual, such as a timeline or comparison.
Build a mid-quiz screen that shows that visual using only the shopper's own entered data.
Do not add any simulated or invented projection to the visual.
A/B test the quiz with this screen against the quiz without it.

test.method: A/B test the quiz with the personalized progress visual against the version without it.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Show a real percentile comparison against other quiz-takers' answers
hypothesis: If a quiz screen shows a real percentile comparison against other quiz-takers' actual measured answers, then the shopper gets a genuine positive feeling instead of a generic encouragement line, but only when the comparison is backed by a real measured base.

signal.check: A quiz has enough answer volume to compute a real percentile on at least 1 question, but currently shows only generic encouragement copy.

risk.note: Never invent a percentage; compute it only from the store's own real answer data.

prerequisites: Enough quiz answer volume to compute a real percentile on at least 1 question
steps: Pick 1 quiz question with enough answer volume to compute a real percentile.
Compute the shopper's percentile against the real measured answer distribution.
Show it as a short positive line at that point in the quiz.
Recompute periodically as the answer base grows.

test.method: A/B test the quiz with the real percentile screen against the version with generic encouragement copy.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Add a commitment pop-up right before the quiz offer reveal
hypothesis: If a quiz shows a short pop-up right before the offer reveal that asks the shopper to explicitly commit to an action, then the shopper's intent is locked in before price shows, instead of the offer being the first ask after a long quiz.

signal.check: A quiz goes straight from the last question or loading screen into the offer with no explicit commitment step.

risk.note: Keep the commitment choice honest; do not force a choice with no real alternative option.

prerequisites: A quiz builder that supports an interstitial screen before the results page
steps: Add 1 screen right before the offer reveal.
Ask the shopper to choose a simple, honest commitment statement, such as agreeing to try the recommended step.
Give a real alternative option, not a forced single choice.
A/B test the quiz with this screen against the quiz without it.

test.method: A/B test the quiz with the commitment pop-up against the version without it.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Check a quiz taker's target date against real delivery estimates
hypothesis: If a quiz asks for a target event or need-by date and compares it to real delivery and shipping estimates, then the shopper is warned about an unrealistic timeline or offered expedited shipping before they buy, instead of finding out after ordering.

signal.check: A quiz or PDP asks about a target date or occasion but never checks it against real shipping and delivery times.

risk.note: Requires accurate, current shipping estimates; a wrong estimate is worse than no check.

prerequisites: Real, current delivery and shipping estimates by destination
steps: Ask the shopper for a target event or need-by date where timing matters.
Compare that date to the real current delivery estimate for their destination.
If the timeline is tight or unrealistic, show a warning or recommend expedited shipping.
Keep the delivery estimate data current as shipping times change.

test.method: Compare return, refund and support-ticket rates for orders with and without the delivery check.
test.read_point: After 1 full fulfilment cycle

title: Recommend a starter pack size from quiz routine or consumption answers
hypothesis: If a quiz's routine or consumption answers are used to recommend a starter pack size or subscription frequency, not just which product, then consumable or replenishable SKUs get a sizing recommendation that fits real usage instead of a default size.

signal.check: A product quiz recommends only which SKU to buy, with no logic connecting routine or usage answers to pack size or subscription frequency.

risk.note: The sizing rule must be honest; do not push a larger size than the stated usage supports.

prerequisites: Quiz questions on routine, frequency or amount used
A defined rule mapping usage to pack size or frequency
steps: Add or use existing quiz questions on how often or how much the shopper expects to use the product.
Write a simple rule mapping those answers to a recommended pack size or subscription frequency.
Show the recommended size or frequency on the results page, with an easy way to change it.
A/B test the sizing recommendation against a single default size.

test.method: A/B test the quiz with sizing recommendation against showing only a default size.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Derive the page's persuasion frame from quiz answer clusters
hypothesis: If the page's persuasion frame, whether expert-led, proof-heavy or logic-led, is chosen from clusters in quiz answer data and applied consistently across ads, quiz screens and the sales page, then the whole funnel speaks in 1 voice instead of drifting between frames.

signal.check: A brand's ads, quiz and sales page use different persuasion frames with no data behind the choice.

risk.note: The frame must be based on real answer clusters, not the marketer's preference.

prerequisites: Quiz answer data with enough volume to cluster
Exported answer data by segment
steps: Export quiz answers and cluster them by skepticism, aspiration or rational-objection signals.
Pick the dominant frame that fits the largest or most valuable cluster: expert-led, proof-heavy or logic-led.
Apply that same frame's tone and proof choices across ads, quiz screens and the sales page.
Re-check the dominant cluster periodically as traffic and targeting shift.

test.method: A/B test the consistently-framed funnel against the current mixed-frame funnel.
test.read_point: After the test reaches a meaningful spend level

title: Check quiz-derived audience mix against the intended avatar
hypothesis: If the age and awareness mix read from quiz answers is compared to the brand's intended target avatar, then a mismatch points to fixing ad creative or targeting instead of rebuilding a page that was never the real problem.

signal.check: Quiz answer data on age or prior product experience differs noticeably from the avatar the brand's ads are meant to target.

risk.note: This is a diagnostic step; the fix it points to (creative or targeting) sits outside the page itself.

prerequisites: Exported quiz answers on age, demographics and prior experience
A written description of the intended avatar
steps: Export the age and awareness-related answers from the quiz.
Compare the mix to the avatar the brand's ads and targeting are meant to reach.
If they mismatch, review ad creative and targeting before changing the page.
Re-run the comparison after any targeting change.

test.method: Compare cost per acquisition before and after correcting a targeting mismatch found this way.
test.read_point: After the targeting correction has run for a full cycle

title: Use a soft demand-implying CTA only when stock is genuinely limited
hypothesis: If a cold-traffic advertorial uses a soft CTA that implies demand, such as 'check availability', instead of a hard 'buy now', then the softer ask can raise clicks, but only when stock or demand is genuinely limited so the implication is honest.
does_not_apply_when: Stock or demand is not actually limited

signal.check: A cold-traffic advertorial uses a hard 'buy now' CTA on a product where a softer, demand-implying frame has not been tested, or is considering 'check availability' with no real stock limit to back it.

risk.note: Never use a demand-implying CTA when stock is not actually limited; that is a false scarcity signal.

prerequisites: A real, checkable stock or demand limit
steps: Confirm the product's stock or demand is genuinely limited before considering this CTA style.
Write the CTA as a soft, demand-implying line such as 'check availability' rather than 'buy now'.
A/B test it against the current hard CTA on the same page and traffic.
Judge on purchase rate after the click, not click-through alone.

test.method: A/B test the soft demand-implying CTA against the current hard CTA.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Color-code a draft by pain, desire and mechanism to check the mix
hypothesis: If an advertorial draft is marked in 3 colors for pain, desire and mechanism mentions, then a reviewer can see at a glance whether every section mixes all 3, instead of running long blocks of only pain or only feature copy.

signal.check: A completed advertorial draft has not been checked for whether pain, desire and mechanism appear together throughout, and reads unevenly in places.

risk.note: This is an editing technique with no downside beyond the time it takes.

prerequisites: A completed advertorial draft
steps: Pick 3 colors: 1 for pain mentions, 1 for desire mentions, 1 for mechanism mentions.
Mark every sentence in the draft with its color.
Zoom out and check that each section shows a mix of all 3 colors.
Rewrite any section that is a long block of only 1 color.

test.method: Compare conversion rate for drafts that passed the color-code check against drafts that did not.
test.read_point: After enough drafts have been tested with and without the check

title: Score a page against 4 value-equation parts and fix the weakest
hypothesis: If a page's copy is scored against 4 parts, the dream outcome, the perceived likelihood of achieving it, the time delay to the result, and the effort or sacrifice required, then fixing whichever part scores weakest first raises conversion faster than rewriting the whole page.

signal.check: A page has not been scored against the 4 value-equation parts, and edits so far have been made without knowing which part is weakest.

risk.note: Scoring is subjective; use it to prioritize, not as an exact measurement.

prerequisites: The current page copy to review
steps: Read the page and rate each of the 4 parts: is the dream outcome stated, is likelihood de-risked, is time delay quantified, is effort or sacrifice named.
Rate each part on a simple scale, such as strong, present or missing.
Fix whichever part is weakest first.
Re-score after the fix before moving to the next weakest part.

test.method: A/B test the page after fixing the weakest value-equation part against the current version.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Translate premium product value points into status, not features
hypothesis: If every value point for a premium or status-driven physical good, such as a style trend, delivery speed or white-glove service, is translated into what it does for the buyer's status, then the high price is justified by identity, not a feature list nobody compares line by line.

signal.check: A premium product page lists specifications and service details as plain features with no connection to the status or identity outcome the buyer is really paying for.

risk.note: Status framing must stay honest about what the product and service actually deliver.

prerequisites: A clear picture of the buyer's status motive for this category
steps: List the product's real features and service details: materials, style, delivery speed, installation or white-glove service.
For each, write what it means for the buyer's status or how others will see them, not just the fact itself.
Rewrite the value prop sections around the status translation.
A/B test the status-framed page against the current feature-listed page.

test.method: A/B test the status-framed page against the current feature-led page.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Check a swipe page's ad run time before modeling its structure
hypothesis: If a candidate swipe or reference ad's run time is checked in a public ad library before its structure is used as a model, then a long run time signals it is actually working, instead of assuming any page found online is a proven structure.

signal.check: A team is about to model a competitor or third-party page's structure with no check on how long its feeding ad has actually run.

risk.note: A long run time is a signal, not proof; the page could still be for a very different audience or product.

prerequisites: Access to a public ad library for the relevant platform
steps: Find the candidate swipe page's feeding ad in a public ad library.
Check how long that ad, or its close variants, has been running.
Prefer swipes whose ads have run for weeks or months over ones that appear new.
Model only the structure and pacing, never the text, claims, images or names.

test.method: Compare hook rate for pages modeled on validated long-running swipes against pages modeled on unvalidated ones.
test.read_point: After each modeled page reaches a meaningful spend level

title: Delay the sticky CTA until after the product introduction on long pages
hypothesis: If a long-form advertorial or presell page delays its sticky mobile CTA so it appears only after the reader scrolls past the product introduction, then the button does not interrupt the story before the reader knows what is being sold.

signal.check: A long story-led advertorial or presell page shows a sticky mobile CTA from the top or at the halfway point, before the product has been introduced.

risk.note: Re-check the trigger point whenever the page is edited so it stays tied to the product paragraph.

prerequisites: A page builder or theme that supports a scroll-triggered sticky button
steps: Find the paragraph where the product is first introduced in the story.
Set the sticky CTA to appear only after the reader scrolls past that paragraph.
Confirm it does not show at the top or around the halfway point.
Re-test the trigger position if the page copy is later edited.

test.method: A/B test the delayed sticky CTA against an always-visible sticky CTA on the same page.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Build the advertorial persona from 1 real buyer's own data
hypothesis: If an advertorial's persona is built from 1 real buyer's own order record, ad comment or survey answer, checked against who the brand wants more of, then the story speaks with real specificity instead of a composite or invented avatar.

signal.check: An advertorial's persona is written from an assumed or composite avatar with no single real buyer behind it.

risk.note: Contacting a real buyer for research must follow the brand's privacy and consent rules.

prerequisites: Order or ad-comment data identifying real buyers
A way to learn more about that buyer with consent
steps: Find 1 real buyer from order or ad-comment data who fits the segment the brand wants more of.
Learn more about them through their public comment, an email, or a short survey, with consent.
Write down 1 age, 1 situation, 1 problem and 1 problem length for that specific person.
Check this persona matches who the brand wants to reach at scale before writing the full advertorial.

test.method: A/B test the advertorial built from a real single-buyer persona against the current composite-persona version.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Fix the quiz question with an outlier drop-off spike
hypothesis: If per-question drop-off in quiz analytics is read after launch and 1 question shows a much larger drop than its neighbors, then softening or removing that question fixes the real leak instead of guessing at the whole quiz.

signal.check: A quiz is live with per-question analytics available, but no one has checked whether 1 question causes a disproportionate drop-off.

risk.note: Do not remove a question that is deliberate qualifying friction added on purpose after the quiz is proven.

prerequisites: Per-question drop-off data from the quiz tool
steps: Pull per-question drop-off from the quiz analytics.
Plot or list the drop-off rate for each question in order.
Flag any question with a drop-off far above its neighbors.
Soften the wording or remove that question, unless it is deliberate qualifying friction.
Re-check drop-off after the change.

test.method: Compare quiz completion rate before and after fixing the outlier question.
test.read_point: After enough quiz sessions accumulate on the fixed version

title: Branch the post-quiz email sequence by the shopper's own answers
hypothesis: If quiz-captured leads enter a multi-email nurture sequence branched by their own quiz answers, instead of 1 generic sequence for everyone, then each lead reads follow-up content that matches their stated need, which moves more of them toward purchase.

signal.check: A quiz captures name and email but sends every lead the same generic follow-up sequence regardless of their answers.

risk.note: Branching adds email-flow complexity; keep the number of branches small enough for the team to maintain and test.

prerequisites: An email platform that supports segment or tag-based branching
Quiz answers passed to the email platform as tags or fields
steps: Pick 1 or 2 key quiz answers that meaningfully change what a lead needs to hear.
Pass those answers to the email platform as tags or profile fields.
Build 2 or more short branches of the nurture sequence matched to those answers.
Keep marketing consent separate from the quiz result opt-in.
Compare purchase rate across branches to see which nurture content converts best.

test.method: Compare purchase rate for branched sequences against the current single generic sequence.
test.read_point: After 1 full nurture-sequence cycle

title: Update the product image to match the selected variant
hypothesis: If the product image updates automatically to match the selected color or size on the PDP and in bundle or tier selectors, then the shopper sees exactly what they are choosing instead of a static image regardless of variant.

signal.check: A PDP or bundle selector keeps the same product image no matter which color, size or tier the shopper selects.

risk.note: Requires real photography or renders for every variant combination shown; do not fake a variant's look.

prerequisites: A real product photo or render for each variant shown
A theme or app that supports per-variant image swapping
steps: Confirm a real photo or render exists for each variant combination the selector offers.
Wire the variant selector to swap the main image when color or size changes.
Apply the same pattern to bundle or tier selectors where the pack looks visibly different.
Check the swap works correctly on mobile.

test.method: A/B test the page with variant-linked images against the current static image.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Add an honest best-seller or new badge on collection-grid items
hypothesis: If a small number of proven or fresh items on the collection grid carry an honest 'Best Seller' or 'New' badge, then shoppers browsing many options get a nudge toward items other people already buy, without adding any extra step.

signal.check: A collection grid shows no badges at all, or badges are inconsistent with which items actually sell best or are newest.

risk.note: Only badge items that are genuinely best sellers or genuinely new; a false badge is a deceptive practice.

prerequisites: Real sales data to identify actual best sellers
A real launch date to identify actually new items
steps: Pull sales data to identify the store's real best-selling items in each collection.
Identify items that are genuinely new within a recent window.
Add an honest badge to those items only, not to most of the grid.
Refresh the badges periodically as sales data and new launches change.

test.method: A/B test the collection page with honest badges against the version without them.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Add a spend-to-unlock progress bar inside the cart drawer
hypothesis: If the cart drawer shows a progress bar toward a discount, free shipping or gift threshold, then shoppers can see exactly how much more to add to unlock it, which nudges basket size up without a hard upsell pitch.

signal.check: The cart drawer shows items and a checkout button but no visible progress toward any spend-based threshold the store already offers.

risk.note: Model the threshold against margin and AOV distribution first; an unlock set too low gives away margin for no real lift.

prerequisites: A real free-shipping, discount or gift threshold the store can honor
Margin and AOV data to set the threshold
steps: Model the margin impact of the intended threshold against current AOV distribution.
Add a progress bar inside the cart drawer showing the gap to that threshold.
Update the bar live as items are added or removed.
A/B test the cart drawer with the progress bar against the current cart drawer.

test.method: A/B test the cart drawer with the progress bar against the current cart drawer, watching AOV and margin together.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Pair every press logo with a short quote from that outlet
hypothesis: If every 'as seen in' press or media logo is paired with a short quote of what that outlet actually said about the brand, then the proof carries real weight instead of reading as a bare, unverifiable logo strip shoppers have grown numb to.

signal.check: A page shows a row of press or media logos with no quote or attribution next to any of them.

risk.note: Only use a real, attributable quote the brand can point back to; never invent or paraphrase press coverage.

prerequisites: Real press or media coverage with a quotable line
steps: Find the real coverage behind each press or media logo shown on the page.
Pull a short, accurate quote from each piece of coverage.
Place the quote next to its logo instead of showing a bare logo strip.
Remove any logo with no real, findable coverage behind it.

test.method: A/B test the page with quoted press logos against the current bare logo strip.
test.read_point: After the test reaches the page's traffic floor

title: Build a save-worthy reference asset instead of only sales copy
hypothesis: If a store builds a reference-style asset, such as a buying guide, size chart or pairing guide, useful enough that a shopper would save or print it, then the content page earns organic reach and repeat visits beyond what pure sales copy attracts.

signal.check: A store's content pages are all sales-focused with no standalone reference asset a shopper would want to keep or share.

risk.note: The asset must be genuinely useful on its own, not a thin wrapper around a sales pitch.

prerequisites: A real category question the asset can answer well, such as sizing, pairing or care
steps: Pick a real question shoppers have that a guide, chart or reference page can answer well.
Build it to be useful even to someone not ready to buy yet.
Keep brand promotion light within the asset.
Publish it as its own page and track organic traffic and shares to it.

test.method: Track organic clicks and shares to the reference asset over time.
test.read_point: After the asset has been live for at least 1 full month
